• Indirect warm-ups (using activities not directly related to the sport, such as cycling and stretching) can often 
enhance performance if kept at an unstrcssful level
• Almost all studies which show warming up to be detrimental used untrained subjects who apparently cannot 
tolerate high-intensity warmups
• Strenuous, non-specific warmups can interfere with sports requiring motor skill
• The selection of a suitable warm-up depends on personal experimentation with different methods in training.
3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle A ctivity
It is known that, if a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its activity slows down more after the last one 
than when it is stimulated by a single impulse. Any stimulus, whether momentary or not, leaves traces in the 
nervous system. The traces or after-effect phenomenon persists for some time after stimulation ceases, which 
reveals the relative inertness of the nervous system and its great significance for motor activities (Pimenov, 1907, 
Pavlov, 1929, Orbeli, 1947). In physiology, this specific form of muscular facilitation (see PNF, Ch 7.2) is 
referred to as post-tetanic potentiation, in particular when the preparatory stimulus is produced by maximal or 
activity or 44tetanus” (e.g. Abbate, 2000; Brown & Euler, 1938;. Burke et al, 1970; Grange et al, 1993; Marsdcn el 
al, 1971; O'Leary et al, 1997; Palmer & Moore, 1989; Vandervoort, 1983). These phenomena and the processes of 
adaptation associated with them form the foundation for fitness development. They determine the continuing rise 
in fitness, despite periodic interruption in the training process (Matveyev, 1964; Mateev 1964; Zimkin, 1965).
Research into the after-effects of muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature. For 
instance, a statistically significant increase in the speed of an unloaded movement was found directly after the 
same movement was executed with a weight (Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962). Conversely, other research 
could not detect such an effect, despite subjective claims by the athletes that their movements felt quicker after 
using loads (Nofsinger, 1963; Nelson & Lamber, 1965). No increase in the vertical jump could be measured 
shortly after preceding resistive exercises (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965). Shot-put results even deteriorated after 
preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
The after-effect has been examined in more detail in Russian research. It has been noted that preliminary 
isometric tension has a positive effect on the subsequent dynamic work. Despite fatigue following isometric 
tension, the effectiveness of dynamic work increases, usually by up to 20% when compared with work executed 
without preliminary isometric tension. 
With the reverse sequence of work, results deteriorate (Shiedin & 
Kunevich, 1935; Vinogradov & Delov, 1938; Vereshchagin, 1956; Farfel, 1964; Uflyand, 1965).
The after-effect occurs immediately after preliminary isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still 
retains some trace of inhibitory influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared 
with its initial level (Leinik, 1951; Vinogradov, 1966). The data indicates that isometric tension under certain 
conditions can serve as a stimulus for dynamic work and play an important role in developing muscular strength.
Dynamic work with heavy weights (i.e. high tension with relatively few repetitions) also elicits a positive 
after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS), which produces a general toning influence on the motor 
apparatus and an improvement in speed and strength (Portnov, 1955; Ratov, 1957; Diachkov, 1961; Muravov 
& Tkachev, 1964; Letunov, 1965).
In practice, the after-effect phenomenon of strength work is used to exploit its immediate and delayed effects. 
It should be noted that there is an improvement in performance immediately following strong tension; i.e. this is 
an immediate after-effect. In addition, intense preliminary strength tension improves results in jumping exercises 
(Diachkov, 1958; 1961; Verkhoshansky, 1961; Tatian, 1964; Tkachev, 1967), in shotputting (Fritsch, 1961; 
Ivanova, 1964; Markov, 1966), and in rowing (Ermishkin & Vozniak, 1965; Chuprun, 1966).
For the delayed effects, preliminary stimulation is used to improve the functional state of the neuromuscular 
apparatus during the athlete's preparation for competition or in training for speed-strength (Diachkov, 1961; 
Vrzhesnevsky, 1964; Khodykin, 1976). The positive effect is obtained only if this state is promoted at an 
optimal level of stimulation. Over-excitation of the CNS has a negative effect on the precision and coordination of 
movements, i.e. on athletic skill (Diachkov, 1961; Yakimova, 1964).
The after-effect phenomenon in the nervous system and its influence on the subsequent work is influenced by 
many factors, in particular, the strength of the stimulus, fatigue and the time interval separating the preceding 
activity from the subsequent activity. Thus, after tonic work (with barbell squats) the following changes in the

3.4.3 Additional Movement
Some experienced coaches judge the mastery of a sprinter by the action of his jaws. If the teeth are clenched and 
the face has a strained expression during a race, then the level of proficiency is regarded as low. If the jaw is 
relaxed and the face is calm, then their movements are fluid and unconstrained and the athlete displays the skill for 
running fast. Although subjective, it is a reasonably accurate evaluation of mastery in cyclic movements when the 
muscles work in a rapid sequence of tension and relaxation. Clinically, this observation would appear to relate, at 
least in part, to the TMJ (tempcro-mandibular joint) syndrome sometimes treated by physical therapists to 
relieve muscular stress in various parts of the body which are distant from the jaw.
However, in acyclic movements requiring the display of powerful force, it is not possible to evaluate 
proficiency in this way. In this case, muscular force is concentrated in a single instantaneous contraction and even 
the anatomical antagonists may function as synergists. Under these conditions, the so-called additional movement 
contributes to raising the working effect. In physiotherapeutic PNF (see 7.2), this phenomenon is regarded as a 
consequence of what is termed overflow or irradiation from stronger to weaker or more fatigued muscles (Knott & 
Voss, 1968).
Muscular activity (an indicator of electrical excitation) is dependent not only on the processes taking place 
within the prime movers, but also on the state of the other muscle groups. Both unloaded and loaded movements 
with large resistance elicit electrical activity in the unexercised musculature of the body (Farfel, 1961; Levin, 1964; 
Sills & Olson, 1958). Furthermore, the strength and endurance of the arm musclcs executing dynamic work 
increase significantly by including other skeletal muscles in the work (Gorbunova & Khabarova, 1955; 
Mukhamedova, 1958). Exercising the muscles on one side of the body causes an increase in strength on the 
unexercised side, i.e., the well-known 'cross training' phenomenon (Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; 
Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988).
Thus, an additional movement which does not serve to increase the economy of the motor action, has a 
specific physiological value and its systematic involvement can be very useful.
The combination of two or several muscle groups involved simultaneously or sequentially offers several 
advantages. Thus, the amount o f force developed by the right arm is significantly influenced by the muscles 
taking part in the additional movement: a momentary contraction of the extensors of the left elbow increases the 
strength and speed of the flexors of the right elbow to a larger degree than a contraction of the left elbow flexors 
(Mukhammedova, 1958). If, during rhythmic flexing of the right arm, the extensors of the left are momentarily

tensed, then the work capacity of the right arm will increase by 39-42%; if the flexors of the left arm are tensed, it 
will decrease by 8-22%. Tensing the extensors of the left arm after first fatiguing the flexors of the right, increases 
the capacity of the latter to do significantly more work. Tensing the flexors o f the left arm has no effect in this 
case (Popov, 1938).
Thus, the change in the work capacity of one muscle group by recruiting others into the work depends on 
many factors and varies under different circumstances. The athlete's fitness, the type of muscular activity during 
the additional dynamic or static work, as well as a decrease or increase in the load and work rhythm all influence 
the working effect (Vinogradov, 1966). Thus, in the above-mentioned experiments by Mukhammedova, a large 
stimulatory effect is obtained when the additional effort of the left arm reaches 25-33% of that of the right arm.
Finally, results are determined by the functional state of the motor system. Research indicates that, to obtain 
a definite stimulatory effect, the appropriate motor centre in the brain should be in a state of stable excitation and 
reactiveness. The excitation of one neurocentre stimulates this process in the other motor centres, if the latter 
centres become significantly dominant.
Thus, tension in the additional muscle groups increases the excitability of the dominant centre because of the 
afferent impulses coming from them and enhances the effector process in the fundamental muscle groups. The 
basis for this dominance phenomenon is obvious: in the initial stages of work when dominance is still only 
forming, involvement of the other muscle groups will be counter-productive. The effect appears only after some 
time has passed, when dominance has already been established (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya, 1955).
In athletics there are examples where the motor effect is produced (while using additional movement) by the 
dominant centre and by clearly mechanical factors. This is observed in exercises involving a take-off from a 
support using rotary movement (e.g. pole-vaulting). In this case the concentration of muscular excitation, which 
is crucial for rotational acceleration of the body's links, enhances excitation of the dominant centre, thereby 
involving the key element of the take-off, namely the action of the extensor muscles. At the same time, reactive 
force resulting from muscle stretching during the amortisation phase increases the power of the muscles executing 
the take-off (for example, by an average of 25% in the vertical jump). Thus, additional movement is an example 
of the body's adaptive capability, playing a useful role when it becomes necessary to produce maximal tension. 
Clearly, it has a place in strength training.
3.4.4 Preparatory M ovem ent
If one attempts to execute a vertical jump from a half-squat position, it will become immediately obvious that this 
is very difficult without a preliminary movement. Considerable muscle tension will be needed to restrain the 
natural preparatory movement which man consciously or unconsciously resorts to each time he is preparing to 
execute an action requiring the production of significant force.
The preparatory movement is different in each specific case, depending upon the situation and the given 
motor task. However, the objective is still the same, i.e. to increase the working range and prepare the muscles for 
a more powerful effort. The latter is accomplished by stretching the muscles, which produces a strong motor 
impulse via the myotatic reflex and creates additional elastic tension.
The fact that preliminary muscular tension precedes an effort requiring the intense production of strength has 
been noted in several investigations using EMG analysis (Salchenko, 1960; Kotelnikov, 1966; Popov, 1968; 
Asmussen & Bonde-Peterson, 1974). Obviously one should not conclude that preliminary muscle tension is 
always necessary for the execution of exercises. Preliminary tension can be appropriate if it is well timed and 
immediately precedes the working-effort, or if it is accomplished during the preparatory movement and its 
magnitude is optimal. Thus, it may be appropriate to use preparatory movements when it is necessary to produce 
great strength and speed, as well as to enhance the economy of a motor action.
3.4.5 Coordination in Muscular Work
Even with relatively simple movements, the same effect can be produced through many different combinations of 
the muscles involved. A typical working effect in non-standard muscular work was observed , where the external 
display of this typical working effect varies with the amplitude, speed and strength of the movement (Fidelius, 
1959; Zhukov & Zakhariants, I960; Zimkin, 1962; Ratov, 1962). Thus, the impulse (F.t) o f the vertical jump 
take-off varies according to the force F and the duration t of its action. The greater the athlete's fitness, the more 
stable the magnitude of the impulse, and the more stable the distribution of force over time (Verkhoshansky, 
1963; Arutyunyan, 1964). Therefore, during a given exercise, the ineffective and weakly effective variants of

(Zimkin, 1962; Korobova, 1964). Well-prepared athletes use only those combinations which enable them to use 
their motor potential most efficiently.
Changes in the character of muscular activity during the execution of movement can occur in several forms 
(Averianov, 1963; Moikin, 1964):
• changc in the sequence of different muscle groups participating in the movement
• change in the number of muscle groups participating in the movement
• change in the relative degree of participation of different muscles in the movement.
In cyclic movements, the duration of the active and relative rest phases changes (Kuchin, I960; Ratishvili, 1966), 
and the maximal contribution shifts from one group of muscles to another (Lazareva, 1966; Absalyamov, 1968).
Movements associated with overcoming large resistance or executed with great speed characteristically switch 
the activity to the muscles o f the proximal links (Ivanitsky, 1956; Lebedev, 1962; Moikin, 1964), as well as 
produce a differentiation in the activity of different parts of the muscle (Averianov & Shibanov, 1964).
In complex multi-joint movements, the resulting force does not equal the sum of the individual maximum 
tensions of which each of the contributing muscle groups is capable. For example, the largest summatcd force 
which a rower develops is at the beginning of the movement, although at this instant the legs are working at an 
disadvantageous angle in the knee and hip joints (Table 3.9). However, the percentage utilisation of absolute 
strength (the sum of the maximum force that the muscles of the arms, torso and legs develop individually) is 
largest at this moment (Egorov, 1966). 
Thus, the disadvantageous conditions for the work of one muscle can be 
compensated for by the more advantageous conditions for another’s work through the effective coordination of 
contributory actions (in this instance, the back muscles).

3.4.6 Efficiency of Energy Expenditure
The efficiency with which an athlete executes a given movement has a profound effect on the functional use of 
strength, specd-strength, strength-endurance and all other components of fitness. Energy expenditure in any 
individual is affected not only by neuromuscular efficiency, but also by factors such as bodymass and type of 
exercise.
For instance, after the warm-up, the rate of energy expenditure of Class I-III weightlifters varies from under 8 
kjoulcs/min in the 56 kg division to over 23 kJ/min in the +110kg division, while the mean energy expenditure for 
Class I-III weightlifters across all bodymass divisions is 14.8 kJ/min (see Table 3.10). Energy expenditure tends

movement skills in physical training. Tables 3.10 and 3.11 show clearly that elite competitors generally use

# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) and
force-displacement curve F(s) change in a consistent overall pattern: the time to reach
maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves closer
to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases. Verkhoshansky
cites his own longitudinal data (a leg-extension task, before and after 6 months of
training) and several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
support (PDF pp. 109-110, printed pp. 98-99, Figs 2.1-2.3). He then describes four distinct
sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend but differing in where
force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which shortens the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 110-111, printed pp. 99-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; he attributes it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the shared trend (faster force onset, higher peak,
shorter total duration) is consistent with well-replicated modern findings that RFD and
neural drive improve with resistance training independent of large hypertrophy changes,
which would explain the timing shift; the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is better explained by task constraints (available time, external resistance,
and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of the range
the nervous system learns to emphasize.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — A running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an off-season block,
would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more front-loaded braking
phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength improves, distinct from an
offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or isometric mid-thigh pull trace)
would be expected to show a rising peak force with a flatter, less time-compressed profile.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1, the SEC mechanism behind
the stretch-shortening pattern here).

# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975),
Verkhoshansky states that where in the range of motion an athlete trains a single-joint
movement changes how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp.
102-103.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no cellular mechanism in this passage; he treats it as
an established empirical regularity from isometric training-at-a-single-angle studies. **Inference:**
a plausible mechanism (not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most
field-sport athletes) versus one who needs a large gain at one specific, narrow joint angle
that matches a single sport position (e.g. a very specific start-position strength need).
Favor training through, or anchored near, the lengthened position when general transfer
across a range of joint angles is the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from isometric single-joint training studies from the
1970s (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1974; Raitsin & Sarsania, 1975), not from dynamic, multi-joint,
or modern resistance-training methodology; **Inference:** do not assume this angle-specific
transfer pattern applies identically to dynamic full-range lifts (e.g. a full back squat),
where the muscle passes through many angles within a single repetition rather than training
isometrically at one fixed angle. The text also states the *shape* of the force-angle curve
itself does not change fundamentally with training, only the amount transferred across it,
so this claim is about magnitude of transfer, not about reshaping the underlying joint-angle
strength curve.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete doing isometric mid-thigh-pull-style training near
a lengthened hip/knee position would be expected, per this claim, to show more even carryover
to strength expressed at other joint angles than an athlete who only trains isometric holds
in a deep, shortened flexed position, who would gain more at that specific angle but less
elsewhere.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Chapter 1).

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself notes the mechanisms at the chain and system levels are "the same," differing only in
the number of interacting muscle groups, so system-level claims should be checked against
the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more rigorously established
category.

**Example** — A leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level (single knee
joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level (hip, knee, and
ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block trains at the
kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against an external
opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be assumed to fully
transfer to that system-level skill.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; Verkhoshansky reports that Siff's own research at the University of the
Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under non-isokinetic dynamic
conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the resulting dynamic force-angle
curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves obtained statically. The curve
profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and joint orientation: for example,
maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance) elbow flexion does not occur near
90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The
same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves versus curves measured under
unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in the chapter, Verkhoshansky
states directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are unable to measure functional
maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive strength," so it is "futile" to use
them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on sporting preparedness or progress. (PDF
pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15.)

**Why it works** — Isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular
velocity, removing the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage/release, and
multi-joint coordination that dynamic sporting movements actually use; a device that
constrains those variables necessarily measures a different quality than the unconstrained,
explosive, multi-joint action it is often used to represent.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the department runs the isometric seated calf raise and
other isometric tests on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed
90-degree ankle/knee position (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has
no value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance." The
caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests to infer dynamic,
functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak with a slow rate of force development, or measured
at the wrong joint angle for the sport skill, can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive
performance.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — In a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active quadriceps/glute
drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy stored during the
countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being redirected (component
4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak amortization phase is likely
under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused (component 1) training emphasis
would not fix.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] (Chapter 1).

# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky illustrates with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — Maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities
because most sporting actions occur inside a limited time window; an athlete can be strong
in the sense of high peak force yet slow to reach it, or fast to reach a moderate force level
without a high ceiling. Matching training to which of these two qualities the sport actually
uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say, 1RM strength) that the sport's time
constraints never let the athlete express (see
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1, for the
underlying, broadly-replicated basis of this distinction).

**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
work.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
eliminate either quality from a program.

**Example** — A cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break, closing speed)
are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value from
explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once a
baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.

**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]] (Chapter 1).

# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) and
force-displacement curve F(s) change in a consistent overall pattern: the time to reach
maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves closer
to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases. Verkhoshansky
cites his own longitudinal data (a leg-extension task, before and after 6 months of
training) and several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
support (PDF pp. 109-110, printed pp. 98-99, Figs 2.1-2.3). He then describes four distinct
sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend but differing in where
force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which shortens the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 110-111, printed pp. 99-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; he attributes it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the shared trend (faster force onset, higher peak,
shorter total duration) is consistent with well-replicated modern findings that RFD and
neural drive improve with resistance training independent of large hypertrophy changes,
which would explain the timing shift; the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is better explained by task constraints (available time, external resistance,
and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of the range
the nervous system learns to emphasize.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — A running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an off-season block,
would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more front-loaded braking
phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength improves, distinct from an
offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or isometric mid-thigh pull trace)
would be expected to show a rising peak force with a flatter, less time-compressed profile.

[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1),

# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975),
Verkhoshansky states that where in the range of motion an athlete trains a single-joint
movement changes how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp.
102-103.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no cellular mechanism in this passage; he treats it as
an established empirical regularity from isometric training-at-a-single-angle studies. **Inference:**
a plausible mechanism (not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most
field-sport athletes) versus one who needs a large gain at one specific, narrow joint angle
that matches a single sport position (e.g. a very specific start-position strength need).
Favor training through, or anchored near, the lengthened position when general transfer
across a range of joint angles is the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from isometric single-joint training studies from the
1970s (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1974; Raitsin & Sarsania, 1975), not from dynamic, multi-joint,
or modern resistance-training methodology; **Inference:** do not assume this angle-specific
transfer pattern applies identically to dynamic full-range lifts (e.g. a full back squat),
where the muscle passes through many angles within a single repetition rather than training
isometrically at one fixed angle. The text also states the *shape* of the force-angle curve
itself does not change fundamentally with training, only the amount transferred across it,
so this claim is about magnitude of transfer, not about reshaping the underlying joint-angle
strength curve.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete doing isometric mid-thigh-pull-style training near
a lengthened hip/knee position would be expected, per this claim, to show more even carryover
to strength expressed at other joint angles than an athlete who only trains isometric holds
in a deep, shortened flexed position, who would gain more at that specific angle but less
elsewhere.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Chapter 1).

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself notes the mechanisms at the chain and system levels are "the same," differing only in
the number of interacting muscle groups, so system-level claims should be checked against
the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more rigorously established
category.

**Example** — A leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level (single knee
joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level (hip, knee, and
ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block trains at the
kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against an external
opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be assumed to fully
transfer to that system-level skill.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; Verkhoshansky reports that Siff's own research at the University of the
Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under non-isokinetic dynamic
conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the resulting dynamic force-angle
curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves obtained statically. The curve
profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and joint orientation: for example,
maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance) elbow flexion does not occur near
90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The
same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves versus curves measured under
unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in the chapter, Verkhoshansky
states directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are unable to measure functional
maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive strength," so it is "futile" to use
them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on sporting preparedness or progress. (PDF
pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15.)

**Why it works** — Isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular
velocity, removing the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage/release, and
multi-joint coordination that dynamic sporting movements actually use; a device that
constrains those variables necessarily measures a different quality than the unconstrained,
explosive, multi-joint action it is often used to represent.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the department runs the isometric seated calf raise and
other isometric tests on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed
90-degree ankle/knee position (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has
no value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance." The
caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests to infer dynamic,
functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak with a slow rate of force development, or measured
at the wrong joint angle for the sport skill, can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive
performance.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — In a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active quadriceps/glute
drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy stored during the
countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being redirected (component
4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak amortization phase is likely
under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused (component 1) training emphasis
would not fix.

[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] (Chapter 1).

# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky illustrates with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — Maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities
because most sporting actions occur inside a limited time window; an athlete can be strong
in the sense of high peak force yet slow to reach it, or fast to reach a moderate force level
without a high ceiling. Matching training to which of these two qualities the sport actually
uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say, 1RM strength) that the sport's time
constraints never let the athlete express (see
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1, for the
underlying, broadly-replicated basis of this distinction).

**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
work.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
eliminate either quality from a program.

**Example** — A cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break, closing speed)
are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value from
explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once a
baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.
