# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups

**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and his own data, Verkhoshansky describes building a
**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
running 12.1s versus 12.4s), Verkhoshansky extends this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group (how fast each group develops working force, not just its
peak) on top of the raw strength topography. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs
2.16-2.18.)

**Why it works** — A profile organized by muscle group and quality (strength peak, and
separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific groups are underdeveloped
relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single whole-body strength number cannot
show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures why two athletes with equal peak
strength can still differ in performance, since the sport may reward how fast that strength
is expressed more than its ceiling (see
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).

**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real
usability problem, with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data dictionaries listed as
priority unfinished work (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`). **Inference:** this framework is
a direct conceptual match for that stated gap: a sport-specific dynamometric/functional
profile (per position group, not just per vendor) is essentially what the Development Plan's
proposed sport-specific data dictionary would need to support if it is to identify individual
athletes' weak links rather than just report raw device output; this specific mapping is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** building a useful general profile for a sport requires
a reasonably sized sample of athletes at that sport and level to establish what topography is
typical, which most single-team programs (including a college football roster split across
many position groups) will struggle to establish rigorously; a "general profile" built from a
handful of athletes risks reflecting individual variation rather than a real sport-typical
pattern. This is also a resource-intensive, multi-muscle-group testing approach; **Eric's
baseline** elsewhere states inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data and that
data collection has to be judged on cost versus insight (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy
and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`,
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); a full multi-joint dynamometric battery would need to
clear that same cost-versus-insight bar before being added to an already-running testing
menu.

**Example** — Two running backs with equal 1RM back squats and equal CMJ height could still
differ in acceleration if one shows a slower rate of force development specifically at hip
extension; a functional profile built from isometric or force-plate testing at each major
joint action would surface that difference, where a single squat-max or jump-height number
would not.

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,
since they only move a single limb against gravity).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** use the strength-quality order (absolute, then explosive,
then starting-strength) as a rough sequencing guide within a periodized plan, consistent with
the classic strength-to-power progression already in Eric's baseline: **Eric's baseline:**
off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first, with
already-strong athletes shifting more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). **Inference:** this claim adds a further,
specific step this baseline does not name: starting-strength (the ability to build force
fastest right at the onset of contraction) is described here as the *last* quality to develop
significantly, tied specifically to near-competition-intensity sport-specific work rather
than general strength or speed-strength training; a plan that stops at speed-strength work
may be leaving starting-strength underdeveloped without adding sport-specific,
near-competition-intensity exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from a small number of Soviet single-sport case studies
(pole vault, shot put, plus unnamed jumpers/sprinters), not a broad multi-sport sample;
**Inference:** do not assume the exact muscle-group sequence (e.g. ankle before hip before
knee) generalizes unchanged to football-specific skills, which load the ankle, hip, and knee
in different relative proportions than pole vaulting or shot put. The strength-quality order
(absolute, then explosive, then starting-strength) is also stated to hold mainly for "sports
where the athlete overcomes relatively small resistance, and where the speed of producing
working force ... is most important" (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114), which does not obviously
describe heavy-resistance line-play skills.

**Example** — A freshman football player early in a strength program would be expected, per
this claim, to show his fastest early gains in general/absolute strength; explosive-strength
gains (jump, throw-type output) should follow once absolute strength is established; and
the sharpest gains in true starting-strength (getting off the ball fast at the snap) should
be expected latest, once near-game-intensity technical and speed work is added, not from
weight-room strength work alone.

**Related** — [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (Chapter 1, the
biochemical-level version of the same named phenomenon),
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]].

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), Verkhoshansky reports several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). He also notes it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but states this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation is the conditioned-reflex model of learned
muscular activity: training builds an extensive background of "temporary connections" that
different combinations of motor activity can later draw on, and in early training these
qualities develop somewhat separately before becoming integrated through sport-specific
movements that are structurally similar to them. **Inference:** this is functionally the same
underlying idea as the more detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the author himself defers that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude.

**Example** — A young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and conditioning
work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general strength and
conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his sport-specific
qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to be replaced by
increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1).

# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky states there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is weakly associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). He extends the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height. (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author gives the mechanical chain explicitly for the
jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
reading, consistent with
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
connected quality) haven't moved either.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding
(Verkhoshansky, 1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that
increasing absolute strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are
not directly, statistically connected in the samples studied; **Inference:** modern sprint
literature is genuinely mixed on how much heavy strength training transfers to sprint speed
at different training ages, and some modern sources treat this relationship as more
context-dependent (training age, starting strength level) than this passage implies; treat
this claim as one data point in that broader, still-unsettled discussion, not a settled
modern consensus. Do not use it to justify dropping strength training for speed-dependent
athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still requires the strength link to
function.

**Example** — A defensive back who adds significant back-squat strength but shows no change
in CMJ height or jump-derived impulse would not be expected, per this claim, to see much
carryover to sprint speed either; the more useful readiness signal for expected sprint
improvement is the jump-performance metric, not the strength-test number itself.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Chapter 1).

# Four Ways Two Motor Abilities Can Be "Connected": General/Partial, Essential/Non-Essential, Positive/Negative, Direct/Indirect

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,
Khodykin 1976) gives a four-axis taxonomy for describing how any two motor abilities relate
to each other statistically and functionally: **general vs. partial** (a general connection
is the interaction between two abilities including the influence of all other abilities; a
partial connection isolates the interaction between just those two, controlling for others;
partial contribution is "the most typical case" lower than general, and partial connections
between the same two abilities tend to be more stable across different sports than general
ones); **essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which
efficient sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious
connections that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one
ability assists or hinders another; positive connections are most typical at the general
level, but a positive general-level connection can become negative at the partial level, e.g.
short- and long-distance running, or absolute strength versus speed of movement against small
resistance, are repeatedly found negatively connected); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct
connection links two abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a
third ability C, with no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). (PDF pp.
128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a unifying physiological mechanism for why
these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
transfer.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to interpret why a strength test doesn't correlate with
a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in
[[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]).
**Inference:** before concluding "strength doesn't matter for this skill" from a flat direct
correlation, check whether an indirect path through a more proximate quality (power, RFD,
technical efficiency) exists.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this taxonomy describes correlational patterns from
Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
arbitrary chain of associations.

**Example** — Absolute grip strength and 40-yard-dash time likely show a weak or negative
*direct/partial* connection (little to no useful transfer path), while absolute leg strength
and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated
through jumping ability (see linked claim below).

**Related** — [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]],
[[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]],
[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1).

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (1977) models an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122, Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author does not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces (e.g. general conditioning or
mobility work that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from degrading speed quality).
**Inference:** this maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

**Example** — For a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be "get-off speed and
initial force at the snap." The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's
get-off (the negative-influence case named in the text), some levelling element (e.g.
continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength block) would be needed to
keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

######## claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

topic: eccentric vs concentric force and energy cost
category: [strength, biomechanics, plyometrics]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Eccentric Actions Produce More Force and Cost Less Energy Than Concentric, by Specific Cited Margins

**What it is** — Three related, separately-sourced findings on eccentric versus concentric
muscular work: (1) **Force**: a maximal overcoming (concentric) contraction produces
1.2-1.6x less force than the same muscle displays resisting a stretch (eccentric), per
Bethe (1929); cited examples of eccentric-over-concentric superiority are 22% for the
arms, 46.8% for the forearms, and 50% for the knee extensors. Semyonov's 1968 data on
untrained subjects gives maximal isometric knee-extensor force at 120° as 465 N versus 401
N concentric; combined-regime testing found the largest force (506 N) for slow eccentric
action following preliminary maximal isometric tension, and 453 N for eccentric following
preliminary concentric work. (2) **Energy cost**: eccentric work uses roughly half the
energy of concentric work, but only at slow movement velocities not exceeding 0.12 m/s
(Chauveau, 1904; corroborated by later work: Fenn 1924, Hartree & Hill 1928, Hill 1930,
Cattel 1983); the advantage does not extend to fast, powerful concentric-style movements.
(3) **Reflex mechanism**: the myotatic stretch reflex strengthens with the speed of the
stretch (Samoyloff & Kisseleff 1928; Foerster & Altenburg 1933; Lippold 1957), and better-trained
athletes use this reflex tension more precisely and efficiently during eccentric work
(Zakharyents, 1962). (PDF pp. 136-137, printed pp. 125-126, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for (1) and (3): the myotatic
stretch reflex adds reflexive muscular tension on top of the passive/mechanical resistance
of stretched tissue, and this stretch-driven force addition scales with stretch speed. For
(2), the text does not give a mechanistic explanation beyond citing the calorimetric/heat
studies. **Inference:** a plausible explanation, not stated anywhere in the book, is that
fewer cross-bridges cycle per unit of force produced during slow forcible lengthening than
during shortening; this is offered here only as a plausible guess, not a cited finding.

**When to apply** — Useful as a citable, quantified starting point for programming
eccentric-emphasis work (e.g. eccentric overload machines, tempo-eccentric lifting,
eccentric hamstring work) where the goal is either a large force stimulus at relatively
low metabolic/cardiovascular cost, or building the reflex-tension precision the text
associates with trained athletes. **Eric's baseline:** none of the corpus's testing or
programming documents specify eccentric-only protocols, so this is a gap this text could
inform if the department wants a citable rationale for adding eccentric-emphasis blocks.

# Eight Types of Muscular Tension, Classified by How and How Fast Force Is Displayed

**What it is** — Beyond the basic mechanical regimes (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic,
isokinetic, quasi-isometric; already covered in Ch1, see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]), Siff and Verkhoshansky classify the
*character* of muscular tension in sport into at least eight types, organized by how
quickly tension develops, its magnitude, duration, repetitions, and the muscle's
pre-working state: **tonic** (large, prolonged tension where speed of development doesn't
matter much, e.g. holding a pin in wrestling or a barbell overhead); **phasic** (cyclic,
rhythmic tension-relaxation, e.g. rowing, swimming, cycling, distance running); **phasic-tonic**
(switching between dynamic and stabilizing work within one skill, e.g. gymnastics,
judo, wrestling); **explosive-isometric** (large resistance overcome, force maximum reached
isometrically at the end of the movement, e.g. snatching or jerking a barbell, and the
brief eccentric-to-concentric transition in plyometrics); **explosive-ballistic** (small
relative resistance, force peaks early/mid-movement then the load coasts on inertia, e.g.
shotput, javelin, tennis serve); **explosive-reactive-ballistic** (same as ballistic but with
a sharp, pronounced preliminary stretch immediately before the concentric phase, e.g. some
throws, wrestling and volleyball actions); and two **speed types** — acyclic (a single quick
momentary contraction, e.g. a boxing punch) and cyclic (repeated actions at a fast tempo
where each cycle's working effect must be sustained, e.g. sprinting). (PDF pp. 136-140,
printed pp. 125-129, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work," Fig 3.1; explicitly credited as
Siff & Verkhoshansky's own convenience classification, not an exhaustive or definitive
taxonomy — "we do not pretend to have classified all the forms.")

**Why it works** — The authors argue this classification exists because a "universal
regime of muscular work to develop strength" doesn't exist: which regime dominates a
given sport skill depends jointly on the magnitude, duration, and speed of tension
required, so training method selection has to be matched to the specific tension-type a
skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy — several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one
category can be as misleading as ignoring the distinction altogether. Do not use this as a
testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — A boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure quickness) versus a
heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back (explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary
stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look superficially similar but sit in different cells
of this classification, implying different primary training levers (reaction/movement
time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style work for the power punch).

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (the underlying mechanical
regimes this classification builds on); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(explosive-isometric tension's plyometric transition phase); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the force-time analysis that follows for explosive-type tensions).

# Reaction Time Is Largely Fixed by Genetics; Movement Time Is What Training Actually Changes

**What it is** — "Quickness" (rapid CNS-driven muscle contraction/relaxation without
preliminary stretch, against negligible resistance) is measured as **reaction time**
(stimulus to response/movement-initiation) and is distinct from **movement time** (end of
the reaction phase to end of the movement); the text states no correlation has been
demonstrated between the two (Harbin et al, 1989). Average simple reaction times by
modality: 0.142 s auditory, 0.155 s tactile, 0.194 s visual (Harbin et al, 1989); fully
unpredictable visual signals push reaction time above 0.5 s (Fogel, 1963). Reaction time
splits into a latency phase (stimulus to first EMG activity) and a response phase (EMG
onset to motor action); Hanes & Schall (1996) attribute reaction-time variability to how
fast a monkey's neuronal firing rate reaches a fixed movement-triggering threshold, not to
nerve conduction velocity differences. The text states the **latency period is determined
largely by genetics and minimally affected by training**, so quickness improvement has to
come from the movement/response phase: the average simple unidirectional movement time
(0.3 s) can decrease by more than 50% in highly trained subjects. For complex tasks
requiring anticipation/decision-making (e.g. striking or catching a fast-moving object),
performance depends more on accurately anticipating trajectory than on raw reaction speed
alone. (PDF pp. 144-146, printed pp. 133-135, "Quickness and Reactive Ability.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that latency reflects largely fixed
neural-transmission and central-processing constraints (peripheral sensory-to-CNS and
CNS-to-muscle conduction delays plus a genetically-set neuronal firing-rate threshold),
while movement time (coordination, precision, motor-unit recruitment efficiency once the
decision/signal has fired) is the part of the chain that skill practice and strength/rate-of-force-development
training can actually shorten.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction when interpreting or designing "reaction" drills:
a drill meant to improve true reaction time (auditory/visual go-signal to first movement)
has a hard genetic ceiling and should not be expected to show large gains; a drill meant to
improve movement time (how fast the athlete executes once triggered) is where real,
trainable adaptation is expected. **Inference:** for anticipation-heavy skills (reading a
quarterback's eyes, a running back's cut, a hitter's release point), training time is
better spent on perceptual/anticipation training than on isolated reaction-time drills,
per the text's own point that anticipation ability matters more than raw reaction speed in
these tasks.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific millisecond values (0.142/0.155/0.194 s, the 0.3 s
movement-time baseline, ">50%" trainable reduction) come from a single cited source
(Harbin et al, 1989) and general kinesiology-era research; they are reasonable
order-of-magnitude reference points, not individualized benchmarks, and should not be used
to grade a specific athlete's "trainability" against a fixed target. The claim of "no
correlation" between reaction time and movement time is a single citation, not
independently re-verified here.

**Example** — A cornerback whose backpedal-to-break time is slow should be assessed
separately on (a) how fast he identifies/reacts to the receiver's break (largely
fixed) versus (b) how fast he physically executes the hip-turn-and-drive once triggered
(trainable movement time) — conflating the two risks programming reaction drills to fix
what is actually a movement-time or technique problem.

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
anticipation/mental-rehearsal mechanism relevant to the complex-task anticipation point
here); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (the force-side complement to
this quickness/reaction-time discussion within the same 3.2.1 section).

# The "Speed Barrier" Is a Genetic Ceiling, Not a Mysterious Neural Block

**What it is** — The classic idea of a "speed barrier" — a plateau caused by monotonous
maximal-effort repetition — is rejected: "research has not found convincing experimental
corroboration" for it. Instead, speed of movement is described as having "an upper limit
that is largely predetermined by genetics," so that the halt in a sprinter's improvement
reflects reaching their individual genetic speed ceiling, not hitting some neural barrier.
Supporting evidence cited: sprinters' propulsive muscles run up to 75% fast-twitch fibre
(Gollnick 1972; Thorstensson et al 1977) versus up to 90% slow-twitch in long-distance
runners (Costill 1973); nervous-system excitability level is independently linked to
individual speed (Gorozhanin 1977; Sultanov 1979; Ilin & Malchikov 1979; Tabachnik et al
1978); economical sprinting recovers roughly 60% of mechanical energy expended per cycle
elastically, with the rest replenished metabolically (Verkhoshansky, 1996, uncited
underlying data); and there is a high correlation (r=0.785) between a muscle's elastic
energy-storage capacity and distance-runner performance specifically. The text also notes
that some sprinters improve mainly via strength increases while their muscle-relaxation
ability stays constant, while other talented sprinters improve mainly via better muscle
relaxation efficiency — two distinct improvement pathways to the same outcome. Practical
implication stated directly: "the preparation of high-class sprinters is associated not so
much with the absolute development of speed as it is with the selection of genetically
gifted people and the efficient organisation of training." (PDF pp. 149-150, printed pp.
138-139, "Speed, Speed-Strength and Quickness.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that speed of movement in cyclic locomotion
depends on complex, whole-system neurophysiological control (not simple, isolated-joint
speed qualities), and multiple independently-genetic factors (fibre-type ratio, CNS
excitability, elastic-energy-return efficiency) jointly cap how fast any one individual can
ultimately move — training can approach that ceiling efficiently, but cannot exceed the
combination of these genetically-set inputs.

**When to apply** — Use this to set realistic expectations for how much a given athlete's
top-end speed can change with training, and to justify individualizing the *pathway* to
speed improvement (strength-driven vs. relaxation/efficiency-driven) rather than assuming
one speed-training template fits all athletes. **Eric's baseline:** this aligns with and
gives a physiological rationale for the department's existing framing that "speed is
harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power" while still being
"the biggest separator between good and great athletes" (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed and
sprint," citing 01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11).

**When NOT to apply** — The specific supporting numbers (75%/90% fibre-type extremes, the
60% elastic-energy-return figure, r=0.785) are drawn from a scattered set of older,
mostly single-study citations across different populations; they illustrate the range and
direction of the genetic-ceiling argument, not precise, individually-applicable targets.
This claim should not be used to argue speed is untrainable — the text explicitly says
training organization still matters for reaching one's genetic ceiling efficiently, only
that it cannot be trained past that ceiling.

**Example** — Two sprinters plateauing at the same 40-time should not automatically get the
same "break the barrier" intervention; per this framework, one may have room to improve via
added strength (if their relaxation efficiency is already good), the other via relaxation/coordination
work (if they are already strong relative to their speed), and testing which lever is
slack matters more than a generic max-velocity block for either.

**Related** — [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (Ch1, fibre-type and
hypertrophy-type background); [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]]
(Ch1, velocity-specific training transfer, a related but distinct specificity claim).

# The Gap Between Absolute Strength and Achieved Force Widens as External Resistance Drops

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" — the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax) — changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs
3.3-3.4.)

**Why it works** — The curves for different loads are described as "precisely superimposed
upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which
the authors attribute to starting-strength being a resistance-independent neuromuscular
ability. **Inference:** a plausible extension, not stated directly in the text, is that
past that initial shared segment, higher loads allow more time for force to keep building
toward So before the limb finishes accelerating, while light loads are already moving (and
thus limiting further force production) before peak force is reached, which would produce
the growing deficit at lower resistance shown in the table.

**When to apply** — Use as a citable, quantified rationale for why maximal-strength testing
(1RM, isometric mid-thigh pull) does not directly predict performance in light, fast tasks,
and why light-load/unloaded-movement testing and heavy-load testing measure increasingly
different things as load drops. **Eric's baseline:** this directly supports the department's
existing testing-battery design logic of using multiple load conditions rather than a
single strength number — e.g., pairing 1RM/isometric strength testing with CMJ and sprint
testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"; force-plate CMJ family per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`) — because this table gives the quantitative reason
a single heavy-load strength number correlates poorly (R=0.316 at 20% load) with light,
fast output.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) built from a
specific leg-press-style task; the four discrete resistance points (80/60/40/20% of So) are
not a continuous, generally-validated curve, and the exact correlation coefficients should
not be extrapolated to other joints, exercises, or populations without re-testing. It also
does not by itself tell a coach what to train — it describes the relationship, not a
training prescription.

**Example** — An athlete with an elite back-squat 1RM but an average CMJ is not necessarily
undertrained; per this table, low-load output (like an unloaded jump, effectively near the
0% end of this curve) is only weakly tied to absolute strength, so the more informative
diagnostic is a light-to-moderate-load force-velocity profile, not the 1RM alone.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Ch1, the SJ-vs-CMJ
field proxy for the same Fmax-vs-Fmm strength-deficit concept, which this table's PDF-page
citation explicitly points forward to); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the four-ability decomposition underlying this same F(t) dataset).

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive
force: **absolute strength (So)** — the strength ceiling; **starting-strength (SS)** — the
ability to develop the greatest possible force at the very start of tension; **acceleration-strength
(AS)** — the ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun; and
**absolute speed (Vo)** — average velocity of an unloaded movement. Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. A discus-thrower factor-analysis
example (Table 3.2, thigh extension) shows the top-ranked factor shifting from starting-strength
at low resisting torque to absolute strength at high torque, with the internal ordering of
all six named factors reshuffling as torque increases. Absolute strength (So) is essentially
uncorrelated with, or mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the
strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp.
140-144, printed pp. 129-133, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve — they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio (Vuorimaa & Komi cited as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978").

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**
(the more genetically-constrained qualities). **Eric's baseline:** this sits underneath
the department's existing use of [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(Ch1) — this Ch3 material supplies the quantified internal structure (four abilities, not
just "RFD vs max force") that could sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics
(mRSI, force-plate driver metrics per the HD ODSF framework) are interpreted for a given
athlete's load profile.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — A lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass) should be judged
mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive back's first-step
reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be judged mainly on
starting-strength and absolute speed markers — the same "explosiveness" label hides two
different training targets.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder — a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).

skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy — several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one
category can be as misleading as ignoring the distinction altogether. Do not use this as a
testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — A boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure quickness) versus a
heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back (explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary
stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look superficially similar but sit in different cells
of this classification, implying different primary training levers (reaction/movement
time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style work for the power punch).

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (the underlying mechanical
regimes this classification builds on); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(explosive-isometric tension's plyometric transition phase); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the force-time analysis that follows for explosive-type tensions).

# Reaction Time Is Largely Fixed by Genetics; Movement Time Is What Training Actually Changes

**What it is** — "Quickness" (rapid CNS-driven muscle contraction/relaxation without
preliminary stretch, against negligible resistance) is measured as **reaction time**
(stimulus to response/movement-initiation) and is distinct from **movement time** (end of
the reaction phase to end of the movement); the text states no correlation has been
demonstrated between the two (Harbin et al, 1989). Average simple reaction times by
modality: 0.142 s auditory, 0.155 s tactile, 0.194 s visual (Harbin et al, 1989); fully
unpredictable visual signals push reaction time above 0.5 s (Fogel, 1963). Reaction time
splits into a latency phase (stimulus to first EMG activity) and a response phase (EMG
onset to motor action); Hanes & Schall (1996) attribute reaction-time variability to how
fast a monkey's neuronal firing rate reaches a fixed movement-triggering threshold, not to
nerve conduction velocity differences. The text states the **latency period is determined
largely by genetics and minimally affected by training**, so quickness improvement has to
come from the movement/response phase: the average simple unidirectional movement time
(0.3 s) can decrease by more than 50% in highly trained subjects. For complex tasks
requiring anticipation/decision-making (e.g. striking or catching a fast-moving object),
performance depends more on accurately anticipating trajectory than on raw reaction speed
alone. (PDF pp. 144-146, printed pp. 133-135, "Quickness and Reactive Ability.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that latency reflects largely fixed
neural-transmission and central-processing constraints (peripheral sensory-to-CNS and
CNS-to-muscle conduction delays plus a genetically-set neuronal firing-rate threshold),
while movement time (coordination, precision, motor-unit recruitment efficiency once the
decision/signal has fired) is the part of the chain that skill practice and strength/rate-of-force-development
training can actually shorten.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction when interpreting or designing "reaction" drills:
a drill meant to improve true reaction time (auditory/visual go-signal to first movement)
has a hard genetic ceiling and should not be expected to show large gains; a drill meant to
improve movement time (how fast the athlete executes once triggered) is where real,
trainable adaptation is expected. **Inference:** for anticipation-heavy skills (reading a
quarterback's eyes, a running back's cut, a hitter's release point), training time is
better spent on perceptual/anticipation training than on isolated reaction-time drills,
per the text's own point that anticipation ability matters more than raw reaction speed in
these tasks.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific millisecond values (0.142/0.155/0.194 s, the 0.3 s
movement-time baseline, ">50%" trainable reduction) come from a single cited source
(Harbin et al, 1989) and general kinesiology-era research; they are reasonable
order-of-magnitude reference points, not individualized benchmarks, and should not be used
to grade a specific athlete's "trainability" against a fixed target. The claim of "no
correlation" between reaction time and movement time is a single citation, not
independently re-verified here.

**Example** — A cornerback whose backpedal-to-break time is slow should be assessed
separately on (a) how fast he identifies/reacts to the receiver's break (largely
fixed) versus (b) how fast he physically executes the hip-turn-and-drive once triggered
(trainable movement time) — conflating the two risks programming reaction drills to fix
what is actually a movement-time or technique problem.

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
anticipation/mental-rehearsal mechanism relevant to the complex-task anticipation point
here); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (the force-side complement to
this quickness/reaction-time discussion within the same 3.2.1 section).

# The "Speed Barrier" Is a Genetic Ceiling, Not a Mysterious Neural Block

**What it is** — The classic idea of a "speed barrier" — a plateau caused by monotonous
maximal-effort repetition — is rejected: "research has not found convincing experimental
corroboration" for it. Instead, speed of movement is described as having "an upper limit
that is largely predetermined by genetics," so that the halt in a sprinter's improvement
reflects reaching their individual genetic speed ceiling, not hitting some neural barrier.
Supporting evidence cited: sprinters' propulsive muscles run up to 75% fast-twitch fibre
(Gollnick 1972; Thorstensson et al 1977) versus up to 90% slow-twitch in long-distance
runners (Costill 1973); nervous-system excitability level is independently linked to
individual speed (Gorozhanin 1977; Sultanov 1979; Ilin & Malchikov 1979; Tabachnik et al
1978); economical sprinting recovers roughly 60% of mechanical energy expended per cycle
elastically, with the rest replenished metabolically (Verkhoshansky, 1996, uncited
underlying data); and there is a high correlation (r=0.785) between a muscle's elastic
energy-storage capacity and distance-runner performance specifically. The text also notes
that some sprinters improve mainly via strength increases while their muscle-relaxation
ability stays constant, while other talented sprinters improve mainly via better muscle
relaxation efficiency — two distinct improvement pathways to the same outcome. Practical
implication stated directly: "the preparation of high-class sprinters is associated not so
much with the absolute development of speed as it is with the selection of genetically
gifted people and the efficient organisation of training." (PDF pp. 149-150, printed pp.
138-139, "Speed, Speed-Strength and Quickness.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that speed of movement in cyclic locomotion
depends on complex, whole-system neurophysiological control (not simple, isolated-joint
speed qualities), and multiple independently-genetic factors (fibre-type ratio, CNS
excitability, elastic-energy-return efficiency) jointly cap how fast any one individual can
ultimately move — training can approach that ceiling efficiently, but cannot exceed the
combination of these genetically-set inputs.

**When to apply** — Use this to set realistic expectations for how much a given athlete's
top-end speed can change with training, and to justify individualizing the *pathway* to
speed improvement (strength-driven vs. relaxation/efficiency-driven) rather than assuming
one speed-training template fits all athletes. **Eric's baseline:** this aligns with and
gives a physiological rationale for the department's existing framing that "speed is
harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power" while still being
"the biggest separator between good and great athletes" (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed and
sprint," citing 01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11).

**When NOT to apply** — The specific supporting numbers (75%/90% fibre-type extremes, the
60% elastic-energy-return figure, r=0.785) are drawn from a scattered set of older,
mostly single-study citations across different populations; they illustrate the range and
direction of the genetic-ceiling argument, not precise, individually-applicable targets.
This claim should not be used to argue speed is untrainable — the text explicitly says
training organization still matters for reaching one's genetic ceiling efficiently, only
that it cannot be trained past that ceiling.

**Example** — Two sprinters plateauing at the same 40-time should not automatically get the
same "break the barrier" intervention; per this framework, one may have room to improve via
added strength (if their relaxation efficiency is already good), the other via relaxation/coordination
work (if they are already strong relative to their speed), and testing which lever is
slack matters more than a generic max-velocity block for either.

**Related** — [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (Ch1, fibre-type and
hypertrophy-type background); [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]]
(Ch1, velocity-specific training transfer, a related but distinct specificity claim).

# The Gap Between Absolute Strength and Achieved Force Widens as External Resistance Drops

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" — the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax) — changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs
3.3-3.4.)

**Why it works** — The curves for different loads are described as "precisely superimposed
upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which
the authors attribute to starting-strength being a resistance-independent neuromuscular
ability. **Inference:** a plausible extension, not stated directly in the text, is that
past that initial shared segment, higher loads allow more time for force to keep building
toward So before the limb finishes accelerating, while light loads are already moving (and
thus limiting further force production) before peak force is reached, which would produce
the growing deficit at lower resistance shown in the table.

**When to apply** — Use as a citable, quantified rationale for why maximal-strength testing
(1RM, isometric mid-thigh pull) does not directly predict performance in light, fast tasks,
and why light-load/unloaded-movement testing and heavy-load testing measure increasingly
different things as load drops. **Eric's baseline:** this directly supports the department's
existing testing-battery design logic of using multiple load conditions rather than a
single strength number — e.g., pairing 1RM/isometric strength testing with CMJ and sprint
testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"; force-plate CMJ family per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`) — because this table gives the quantitative reason
a single heavy-load strength number correlates poorly (R=0.316 at 20% load) with light,
fast output.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) built from a
specific leg-press-style task; the four discrete resistance points (80/60/40/20% of So) are
not a continuous, generally-validated curve, and the exact correlation coefficients should
not be extrapolated to other joints, exercises, or populations without re-testing. It also
does not by itself tell a coach what to train — it describes the relationship, not a
training prescription.

**Example** — An athlete with an elite back-squat 1RM but an average CMJ is not necessarily
undertrained; per this table, low-load output (like an unloaded jump, effectively near the
0% end of this curve) is only weakly tied to absolute strength, so the more informative
diagnostic is a light-to-moderate-load force-velocity profile, not the 1RM alone.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Ch1, the SJ-vs-CMJ
field proxy for the same Fmax-vs-Fmm strength-deficit concept, which this table's PDF-page
citation explicitly points forward to); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the four-ability decomposition underlying this same F(t) dataset).

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive
force: **absolute strength (So)** — the strength ceiling; **starting-strength (SS)** — the
ability to develop the greatest possible force at the very start of tension; **acceleration-strength
(AS)** — the ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun; and
**absolute speed (Vo)** — average velocity of an unloaded movement. Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. A discus-thrower factor-analysis
example (Table 3.2, thigh extension) shows the top-ranked factor shifting from starting-strength
at low resisting torque to absolute strength at high torque, with the internal ordering of
all six named factors reshuffling as torque increases. Absolute strength (So) is essentially
uncorrelated with, or mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the
strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp.
140-144, printed pp. 129-133, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve — they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio (Vuorimaa & Komi cited as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978").

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**
(the more genetically-constrained qualities). **Eric's baseline:** this sits underneath
the department's existing use of [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(Ch1) — this Ch3 material supplies the quantified internal structure (four abilities, not
just "RFD vs max force") that could sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics
(mRSI, force-plate driver metrics per the HD ODSF framework) are interpreted for a given
athlete's load profile.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — A lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass) should be judged
mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive back's first-step
reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be judged mainly on
starting-strength and absolute speed markers — the same "explosiveness" label hides two
different training targets.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder — a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).

---
type: library-entry
