# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — Two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different RC/RSI:
Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the plyometric
training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).
######## framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.2.2"
topic: strength-endurance classification
category: [strength-endurance, testing, terminology]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups) — a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). To compare partial endurance across athletes, relative (bodymass-adjusted)
static or dynamic strength-endurance must be calculated. (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp.
142-144, "3.2.2 Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The absolute/partial distinction resolves the contradiction
mechanistically: an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal strength
(a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while a
relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality — which is why the same construct ("strength-endurance")
produces opposite-signed correlations with strength depending on which type was actually
tested.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests" — this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — A quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a whole roster
measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the same test
at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).

---
type: library-entry

# Muscle State Just Before a Movement Ranks Performance: Stretched > Contracted > Relaxed

**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
isometrically tensioned, dynamically stretched, or "shock"-stretched by rapid braking of a
falling load) changes the working effect of the subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump
experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose across four pre-working conditions in
this order: static half-squat start 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ±
5.0 cm; after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for as little as 10 ms beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement — eliminating *spurious*
tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal preliminary tension
for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided its duration is kept
limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157, printed pp. 144-146,
"3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig 3.14.)

**Why it works** — When muscles start relaxed, they are "not optimally ready to work" and
produce a smaller kinetic effect than their capability; preliminary tension (the
"anticipation tuner" of the neuromuscular system, per Bernstein) and preliminary stretch
both pre-load the neuromuscular system so less time/force is spent simply activating the
muscle before useful work begins, and a genuine stretch additionally banks elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction.

**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or
lift outperforms a fully relaxed static start, and to caution against blanket "stay loose
and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for
Baylor's force-plate testing, this is consistent with running both a static-start (squat
jump) and a countermovement/depth-jump variant in the CMJ family (per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`), since the pre-working state itself is shown here to
be a first-order performance variable, not just methodological noise.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific jump-height numbers (39.0/44.2/48.6 cm) come from one
Verkhoshansky dataset and should not be treated as universal benchmarks; the "stay relaxed"
qualification applies specifically to *spurious* tension in muscles unrelated to the task —
it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.

**Example** — A vertical-jump test protocol that only records a static-squat-start jump
will systematically underestimate an athlete's explosive ceiling relative to a depth-jump
variant, per this ~25% height difference (39.0 to 48.6 cm) found here — the two are not
interchangeable measures of "jump ability."

# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits

**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0) — i.e.
maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
stretch-related (SSC) processes — stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling broadly — it
is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions specifically,
not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off.

**Example** — A force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer data near zero
velocity should not be assumed to predict true 1RM isometric force accurately, per the
Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs at a low, non-zero velocity
rather than at V=0.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically (this is close to modern velocity-based-training guidance for squat-pattern
power work). **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this is a useful citable historical
data point supporting load selection in the 60-70% 1RM range for power-focused squat work,
though it should be triangulated against the department's own velocity-based methods
(Perch) rather than applied as a fixed rule, since VBT data on the specific athlete and
exercise is more direct evidence than this single 1988-era powerlifting dataset.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat); it
should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic lifts, ballistic movements, upper
body pressing) without separate data, and it does not override or replace the classical
25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint contractions that figure was actually
derived from — the two describe different kinds of movement, not contradictory answers to
the same question.

**Example** — Programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power output at "25% of
1RM" (the classical isotonic-model figure) would badly undershoot the load that actually
produces peak power output in the real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond attributing the deviation to the influence
of gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system during cyclic locomotion,
conditions absent from isolated-muscle or single-joint isotonic testing; the practical
takeaway offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling; if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a cyclic-sport
athlete, expect a three-zone pattern rather than a single smooth hyperbola, particularly a
zone where force and velocity move together rather than trading off.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] — the book does not
reconcile all three pictures (Hill's hyperbola, Perrine-Edgerton's low-velocity peak, and
this three-zone cyclic curve) into one unified model, and none of the three should be
treated as the settled, final description of the human force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — A coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to a sprinter's
treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not be surprised if the mid-velocity range shows
force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading off, per this cyclic-specific
finding.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — Two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different RC/RSI:
Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the plyometric
training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups) — a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). To compare partial endurance across athletes, relative (bodymass-adjusted)
static or dynamic strength-endurance must be calculated. (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp.
142-144, "3.2.2 Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The absolute/partial distinction resolves the contradiction
mechanistically: an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal strength
(a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while a
relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality — which is why the same construct ("strength-endurance")
produces opposite-signed correlations with strength depending on which type was actually
tested.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests" — this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — A quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a whole roster
measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the same test
at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).

force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling broadly — it
is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions specifically,
not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off.

**Example** — A force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer data near zero
velocity should not be assumed to predict true 1RM isometric force accurately, per the
Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs at a low, non-zero velocity
rather than at V=0.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).
######## claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift.md

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically (this is close to modern velocity-based-training guidance for squat-pattern
power work). **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this is a useful citable historical
data point supporting load selection in the 60-70% 1RM range for power-focused squat work,
though it should be triangulated against the department's own velocity-based methods
(Perch) rather than applied as a fixed rule, since VBT data on the specific athlete and
exercise is more direct evidence than this single 1988-era powerlifting dataset.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat); it
should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic lifts, ballistic movements, upper
body pressing) without separate data, and it does not override or replace the classical
25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint contractions that figure was actually
derived from — the two describe different kinds of movement, not contradictory answers to
the same question.

**Example** — Programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power output at "25% of
1RM" (the classical isotonic-model figure) would badly undershoot the load that actually
produces peak power output in the real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond attributing the deviation to the influence
of gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system during cyclic locomotion,
conditions absent from isolated-muscle or single-joint isotonic testing; the practical
takeaway offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling; if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a cyclic-sport
athlete, expect a three-zone pattern rather than a single smooth hyperbola, particularly a
zone where force and velocity move together rather than trading off.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] — the book does not
reconcile all three pictures (Hill's hyperbola, Perrine-Edgerton's low-velocity peak, and
this three-zone cyclic curve) into one unified model, and none of the three should be
treated as the settled, final description of the human force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — A coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to a sprinter's
treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not be surprised if the mid-velocity range shows
force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading off, per this cyclic-specific
finding.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).

######## framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.3.3"
topic: strength-speed continuum terminology
category: [terminology, strength-speed, exercise-selection]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).
######## claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.3.4.1"
topic: posture and joint angle effects on strength
category: [biomechanics, technique, testing]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output

**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, maximal knee-extension
force in a seated position occurs at a 160° knee angle (with force depending on hip angle),
but in a supine leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a
100°-140° hip-angle range (Lindeburg, 1964); and knee-extension strength increases 10-12%
when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
which changes the mechanical conditions of work — sometimes advantageously (full force
potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).

**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline:** relevant to any
coaching of the clean/pull pattern in Baylor's strength programming and to interpreting
joint-angle-specific force-plate or isokinetic data (e.g. why a knee-extension test result
at one angle should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or in a different
exercise, per the Lindeburg finding above).

**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
verification.

**Example** — A 9% strength reduction from lateral head tilt alone (Sokolov, 1967) is a
concrete, citable reason to coach a neutral head position during a maximal clean attempt,
beyond generic "keep your head neutral" cueing.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Ch1, the general
torque/leverage principle this claim supplies specific joint-angle examples for);
[[principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal]] (the pelvis-specific continuation
of this same posture discussion, 3.3.4.2).
######## principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.3.4.2"
topic: pelvic tilt and lifting safety
category: [technique, injury-risk, coaching]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26

# There Is No Single "Correct" Pelvic Tilt: The Right Tilt Depends on the Movement Phase

**What it is** — The pelvis is the key link between spine and lower extremities, and
inappropriate orientation can create an unstable or weak base and expose the lumbar discs
to injury, particularly under spinal flexion or flexion-plus-rotation. The text directly
challenges the common fitness-industry instruction that a single "correct" (usually
posterior) pelvic tilt applies to all movement: there is a **lumbar-pelvic rhythm** in
which the appropriate tilt changes synchronously through a lift (Cailliet, 1981), confirmed
by video, force-plate, and EMG analysis of weightlifters and powerlifters. Using the
"iliac crest" convention: **posterior pelvic tilt** is appropriate for sit-ups or lifting
objects from above waist level; **anterior pelvic tilt** is the correct rotation for
squatting, lifting heavy loads off the floor, or toe-touching — and starting a lift or
squat with a *posterior* tilt is specifically flagged as dangerous, since it causes lumbar
flexion and exposes the discs. The pelvis actually rotates in three dimensions (X-axis =
anterior-posterior tilt; Z-axis = side-to-side iliac-crest rocking, natural in walking but
risky if it occurs during squatting, overhead pressing, or deadlifting; Y-axis = rotation
that occurs naturally in walking, running, throwing, and kicking, but is harmful to the
lumbar spine under high load or momentum, especially combined with rotation on other axes).
"Neutral" pelvic tilt is explicitly reframed as a *reference standard* for static
standing/sitting/walking, not automatically "the safest position for all movement." (PDF
pp. 164-166, printed pp. 153-155, "3.3.4.2 Strength, Safety and Pelvic Tilt," Fig 3.22.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly that the purpose of deliberate pelvic tilting
is to maintain neutral lumbar curvature as closely as possible, and that neutral pelvic
position is defined only for static standing, so it changes if the body shifts to leaning,
supine, prone, or other positions. **Inference:** connecting these statements into a single
causal chain, i.e. that a fixed pelvic position therefore cannot preserve neutral lumbar
curvature across different lifting phases and so the tilt itself must change to keep that
protective goal constant, is this entry's own synthesis of separate sentences in the text,
not a single sentence the authors themselves state.

**When to apply** — Use this to correct blanket "posterior pelvic tilt" or "brace neutral"
coaching cues applied identically to sit-ups and to floor-based lifts (deadlift, clean
pull, squat): the text's own biomechanical analysis argues these need opposite tilt cues.
**Eric's baseline:** directly relevant to Baylor's barbell coaching (clean, snatch, squat,
deadlift patterns referenced throughout the S&C curriculum material) and to any staff
in-service on lifting technique cues, since this gives a specific, citable rationale for
differentiating tilt cues by lift and by phase rather than using one universal cue.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Siff's own synthesis built primarily on one cited source
(Cailliet, 1981) plus general biomechanical reasoning, not a randomized or outcome-controlled
study of injury rates under different tilt cues; treat the specific "posterior tilt for
sit-ups, anterior tilt for squats/deadlifts" rule as a reasoned coaching heuristic backed
by video/EMG description, not as a proven injury-prevention intervention with measured
outcomes. It also does not address every possible lifting pattern (e.g. Olympic pulling
positions), where the same reasoning would need to be worked through separately.

**Example** — Cueing a lifter to "tuck the pelvis under" (posterior tilt) at the start of a
deadlift or squat, following generic core-bracing advice borrowed from ab-training cues,
is exactly the error this section warns against — the text argues that specific setup
should use an anterior tilt at the iliac crest instead.

**Related** — [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (the preceding
subsection's general posture-and-force-output findings); [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]
(the next subsection's continuation of the same postural-safety discussion).
######## heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.3.4.3"
topic: head and eye position coaching cues
category: [technique, coaching, injury-risk]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Coach Head and Eye Position Deliberately During Barbell Lifts — It Drives Spinal Reflexes and Balance

**What it is** — Head position has a powerful, largely reflexive effect on posture and
lifting safety. Flexing the neck causes a **reflex relaxation of the back's erector
muscles**, which is dangerous during resisted lifts (squatting, cleaning, deadlifting), so
a deliberate degree of neck extension is needed to facilitate strong erector contraction
during ground-based pulls — but not so much as to hyperextend/hollow the back, which
loads the spinal discs asymmetrically. During skilled Olympic-lift phases, specific head
errors have specific consequences: throwing the head back prematurely during the pull can
pull the bar too far from the body; tilting the head back during the jerk can cause the
lift to be lost forward; tilting the head back to look up at the bar during the snatch's
low-squat fixation can cause the lifter to fall backward and lose the lift; and dropping
the head down during the squat can push the lumbar spine into a hyperflexed, injury-risk
position. Eye fixation is tied to head position: maintaining the neutral spinal position is
easiest when the eyes look nearly straight ahead at a fixed, distant object, and a coach or
teammate moving in the lifter's line of sight can disrupt this fixation and should be
avoided during training and competition. (PDF p. 166 [carrying into printed p. 155-156],
printed pp. 154-155, "3.3.4.3 The Effect of Head Position on Strength.")

**Why it works** — The text states the mechanism directly for the neck-position part only:
neck flexion causes a reflex relaxation of the back's erector muscles, which undermines
trunk stabilization during a loaded lift, while extension is needed to facilitate strong
erector contraction. **Inference:** the text does not explain the eye-fixation guidance
through this same reflex, only that it is "essential" alongside head position; that the two
share one mechanism (gaze driving head position, which then drives the cervical reflex) is
this entry's own connecting inference, not a claim the authors make.

**When to apply** — Use as a specific, mechanism-backed coaching cue set for the squat,
clean, jerk, and snatch: cue a fixed, distant gaze point and a neutral-to-slightly-extended
neck through the pull and receiving positions, and treat "look up" or "drop the head"
cueing as directly consequential for bar path and injury risk, not just posture aesthetics.
**Eric's baseline:** directly usable in Baylor's Olympic-lift-family coaching (clean,
snatch, jerk, and squat instruction referenced across the S&C curriculum material) as a
specific, citable rationale for head/eye coaching points beyond generic "keep your head
up" advice.

**When NOT to apply** — This is coaching-observational synthesis, not an outcome study of
lift success/injury rates tied to head position; treat the phase-specific failure
descriptions (bar drifting from the body, missing the jerk forward, falling backward in the
snatch, hyperflexing in the squat) as plausible, mechanistically-grounded coaching
heuristics rather than quantified, tested probabilities. It also does not address every
lift pattern (bench press cervical hyperextension is mentioned only briefly, in the
adjoining text) with the same depth as the Olympic-lift-family discussion.

**Example** — A lifter who habitually looks up and back during the snatch's overhead squat
receiving position, and repeatedly loses the lift backward, is exhibiting exactly the
failure mode this section attributes to premature backward head tilt — the fix is a fixed,
forward-and-slightly-down gaze target, not simply "sit up straighter."

**Related** — [[principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal]] (the preceding
subsection's pelvis-and-lumbar-safety discussion, same overall posture section);
[[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]] (the following
subsection, on limb alignment and symmetry).
######## claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

category: [testing, technique, injury-risk]
confidence: supported

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate — coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed pp. 155-156, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes, and that isokinetic
symmetry testing measures an isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent
functional, whole-movement asymmetry accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply — direct tension with current Baylor practice.** This claim sits in
real tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection
model explicitly includes symmetry (L/R differences) as an optional force-plate reporting
category (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and force-plate/isokinetic symmetry indices are in active use for
rehab and return-to-play decisions. **Eric's review would be needed** to reconcile this
1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based "correction" with the department's
modern use of symmetry metrics; this entry does not resolve that tension, it only flags it
— the book's objection is specifically to *using an isokinetic ratio to drive a
correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry monitoring for RTP tracking purposes
more broadly, but Eric's own view on where that line falls is not stated anywhere in the

# Allometric Scaling Laws Let You Compare Strength Fairly Across Bodymass (and Height) Classes

**What it is** — Because bodymass scales with the cube of linear body dimensions while
muscle cross-sectional area (and thus force capacity) scales only with the square, maximum
strength (F) and bodymass (B) are theoretically related by F = a.B^(2/3) (Lietzke, 1956,
found a best-fit exponent of 0.6748, close to the theoretical 0.6667). Historical
weight-class-comparison formulas built on this (Hoffman's two-thirds-power formula, the
Austin 3/4-exponent formula, McSorley's and Sinclair's parabolic tables) each had accuracy
limits, especially extrapolating to heavier lifters. Siff (1988) fit sigmoid/power-law
curves to the mean of the ten best all-time lifts per bodymass class (up to ~165 kg) and
found a power-law equation, **Total T = a - b.B^(-c)**, fit weightlifting and powerlifting
records with R > 0.996 in all cases (distinct constants given for weightlifting total,
powerlifting total, squat, bench, and deadlift); separate equations were fit for juvenile
lifters (logistic form) and for women (exponential form). Using these equations, an
athlete's Total can be expressed as a percentage of the world-class total for their exact
bodymass, enabling fair cross-weight-class comparison and longitudinal tracking even as an
athlete's bodymass itself changes. Analysis of the equations shows **relative strength
(strength per unit bodymass) actually peaks at a bodymass of 60-67 kg** in elite
weightlifters/powerlifters, not at either extreme. A related but weaker relationship: for a
given bodymass, taller lifters tend to be *less* strong at elite level (an exponential
height-bodymass equation is given per build class, Table 3.5); and the bodymass-strength
correlation weakens as movement speed increases (0.719 for the slow press vs. 0.706 clean-and-jerk
vs. 0.685 snatch), meaning bodymass predicts maximal-strength lifts much better than
fast, technical ones. (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 155-160, "3.3.5 The Dependence of
Strength on Bodymass," "3.3.6 The Relationship between Strength and Height," Tables 3.3-3.5,
Figs 3.23-3.24.)

**Why it works** — The scaling logic is dimensional analysis, not an empirical fit per se:
strength derives from muscle cross-sectional area (a squared, two-dimensional quantity)
while bodymass derives from volume (a cubed, three-dimensional quantity) for
geometrically-similar bodies, so absolute strength cannot keep pace linearly with bodymass
as size increases. This is the authors' own stated reasoning for the F=a.B^(2/3) relationship.
**Inference:** the text does not itself connect this same cross-sectional-area argument to
the separate height finding (3.3.6) in one sentence; extending the logic that way (a
taller lifter at a fixed bodymass has a thinner build and less muscle cross-section) is
this entry's own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make directly.

**When to apply** — Use the underlying two-thirds-power scaling logic (a dimensional-analysis
argument the authors themselves give, not an appeal to outside literature this entry can
name) whenever normalizing strength testing data across athletes of different
bodymass — e.g. comparing back-squat 1RM across a football roster spanning 180-320+ lb
linemen to skill players is misleading without some bodymass adjustment, and simple
per-kg relative strength (load/bodymass) is itself an approximation that over- or
under-corrects depending where an athlete sits on this curve. **Eric's baseline:** relevant
to the department's stated need for sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data (currently
a named gap per `performance-playbook-development-plan.md` 3.2.3) — a bodymass-adjusted
strength-comparison method, even a simplified version of Siff's approach, would be a
concrete way to build fairer cross-position strength benchmarks for football specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific numeric constants (a, b, c values) are fit to
weightlifting and powerlifting records through 1987-1988 and to Russian weightlifter height
data of that era — they should not be applied directly to football or other sport
populations without refitting to relevant data. The dimensional-analysis argument for the
two-thirds exponent is general reasoning the authors give, but Lietzke's best-fit exponent
(0.6748) and Siff's regression constants are single-dataset fits; the "60-67 kg
relative-strength peak" finding is specific to Olympic/power lifters of that period and
should be treated as illustrative, not directly transferable without refitting.

**Example** — Comparing a 90 kg lifter's 405 kg powerlifting total to a 140 kg lifter's 500
kg total by raw numbers alone favors the heavier lifter; converting each to a percentage of
the world-class total expected at their own bodymass (via Table 3.3's fitted curve) gives a
fairer relative-strength comparison, which is the entire point of this scaling approach.

subsection's parallel age-adjustment method, explicitly combined with this bodymass
adjustment in the book's own worked example); [[claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass]]
(uses the same bodymass-normalization logic for sex comparison).

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output

**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, maximal knee-extension
force in a seated position occurs at a 160° knee angle (with force depending on hip angle),
but in a supine leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a
100°-140° hip-angle range (Lindeburg, 1964); and knee-extension strength increases 10-12%
when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
which changes the mechanical conditions of work — sometimes advantageously (full force
potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).

**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline:** relevant to any
coaching of the clean/pull pattern in Baylor's strength programming and to interpreting
joint-angle-specific force-plate or isokinetic data (e.g. why a knee-extension test result
at one angle should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or in a different
exercise, per the Lindeburg finding above).

**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
verification.

**Example** — A 9% strength reduction from lateral head tilt alone (Sokolov, 1967) is a
concrete, citable reason to coach a neutral head position during a maximal clean attempt,
beyond generic "keep your head neutral" cueing.

torque/leverage principle this claim supplies specific joint-angle examples for);

of this same posture discussion, 3.3.4.2).

# There Is No Single "Correct" Pelvic Tilt: The Right Tilt Depends on the Movement Phase

**What it is** — The pelvis is the key link between spine and lower extremities, and
inappropriate orientation can create an unstable or weak base and expose the lumbar discs
to injury, particularly under spinal flexion or flexion-plus-rotation. The text directly
challenges the common fitness-industry instruction that a single "correct" (usually
posterior) pelvic tilt applies to all movement: there is a **lumbar-pelvic rhythm** in
which the appropriate tilt changes synchronously through a lift (Cailliet, 1981), confirmed
by video, force-plate, and EMG analysis of weightlifters and powerlifters. Using the
"iliac crest" convention: **posterior pelvic tilt** is appropriate for sit-ups or lifting
objects from above waist level; **anterior pelvic tilt** is the correct rotation for
squatting, lifting heavy loads off the floor, or toe-touching — and starting a lift or
squat with a *posterior* tilt is specifically flagged as dangerous, since it causes lumbar
flexion and exposes the discs. The pelvis actually rotates in three dimensions (X-axis =
anterior-posterior tilt; Z-axis = side-to-side iliac-crest rocking, natural in walking but
risky if it occurs during squatting, overhead pressing, or deadlifting; Y-axis = rotation
that occurs naturally in walking, running, throwing, and kicking, but is harmful to the
lumbar spine under high load or momentum, especially combined with rotation on other axes).
"Neutral" pelvic tilt is explicitly reframed as a *reference standard* for static
standing/sitting/walking, not automatically "the safest position for all movement." (PDF
pp. 164-166, printed pp. 153-155, "3.3.4.2 Strength, Safety and Pelvic Tilt," Fig 3.22.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly that the purpose of deliberate pelvic tilting
is to maintain neutral lumbar curvature as closely as possible, and that neutral pelvic
position is defined only for static standing, so it changes if the body shifts to leaning,
supine, prone, or other positions. **Inference:** connecting these statements into a single
causal chain, i.e. that a fixed pelvic position therefore cannot preserve neutral lumbar
curvature across different lifting phases and so the tilt itself must change to keep that
protective goal constant, is this entry's own synthesis of separate sentences in the text,
not a single sentence the authors themselves state.

**When to apply** — Use this to correct blanket "posterior pelvic tilt" or "brace neutral"
coaching cues applied identically to sit-ups and to floor-based lifts (deadlift, clean
pull, squat): the text's own biomechanical analysis argues these need opposite tilt cues.
**Eric's baseline:** directly relevant to Baylor's barbell coaching (clean, snatch, squat,
deadlift patterns referenced throughout the S&C curriculum material) and to any staff
in-service on lifting technique cues, since this gives a specific, citable rationale for
differentiating tilt cues by lift and by phase rather than using one universal cue.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Siff's own synthesis built primarily on one cited source
(Cailliet, 1981) plus general biomechanical reasoning, not a randomized or outcome-controlled
study of injury rates under different tilt cues; treat the specific "posterior tilt for
sit-ups, anterior tilt for squats/deadlifts" rule as a reasoned coaching heuristic backed
by video/EMG description, not as a proven injury-prevention intervention with measured
outcomes. It also does not address every possible lifting pattern (e.g. Olympic pulling
positions), where the same reasoning would need to be worked through separately.

**Example** — Cueing a lifter to "tuck the pelvis under" (posterior tilt) at the start of a
deadlift or squat, following generic core-bracing advice borrowed from ab-training cues,
is exactly the error this section warns against — the text argues that specific setup
should use an anterior tilt at the iliac crest instead.

subsection's general posture-and-force-output findings); [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]
(the next subsection's continuation of the same postural-safety discussion).
