# Coach Head and Eye Position Deliberately During Barbell Lifts — It Drives Spinal Reflexes and Balance

**What it is** — Head position has a powerful, largely reflexive effect on posture and
lifting safety. Flexing the neck causes a **reflex relaxation of the back's erector
muscles**, which is dangerous during resisted lifts (squatting, cleaning, deadlifting), so
a deliberate degree of neck extension is needed to facilitate strong erector contraction
during ground-based pulls — but not so much as to hyperextend/hollow the back, which
loads the spinal discs asymmetrically. During skilled Olympic-lift phases, specific head
errors have specific consequences: throwing the head back prematurely during the pull can
pull the bar too far from the body; tilting the head back during the jerk can cause the
lift to be lost forward; tilting the head back to look up at the bar during the snatch's
low-squat fixation can cause the lifter to fall backward and lose the lift; and dropping
the head down during the squat can push the lumbar spine into a hyperflexed, injury-risk
position. Eye fixation is tied to head position: maintaining the neutral spinal position is
easiest when the eyes look nearly straight ahead at a fixed, distant object, and a coach or
teammate moving in the lifter's line of sight can disrupt this fixation and should be
avoided during training and competition. (PDF p. 166 [carrying into printed p. 155-156],
printed pp. 154-155, "3.3.4.3 The Effect of Head Position on Strength.")

**Why it works** — The text states the mechanism directly for the neck-position part only:
neck flexion causes a reflex relaxation of the back's erector muscles, which undermines
trunk stabilization during a loaded lift, while extension is needed to facilitate strong
erector contraction. **Inference:** the text does not explain the eye-fixation guidance
through this same reflex, only that it is "essential" alongside head position; that the two
share one mechanism (gaze driving head position, which then drives the cervical reflex) is
this entry's own connecting inference, not a claim the authors make.

**When to apply** — Use as a specific, mechanism-backed coaching cue set for the squat,
clean, jerk, and snatch: cue a fixed, distant gaze point and a neutral-to-slightly-extended
neck through the pull and receiving positions, and treat "look up" or "drop the head"
cueing as directly consequential for bar path and injury risk, not just posture aesthetics.
**Eric's baseline:** directly usable in Baylor's Olympic-lift-family coaching (clean,
snatch, jerk, and squat instruction referenced across the S&C curriculum material) as a
specific, citable rationale for head/eye coaching points beyond generic "keep your head
up" advice.

**When NOT to apply** — This is coaching-observational synthesis, not an outcome study of
lift success/injury rates tied to head position; treat the phase-specific failure
descriptions (bar drifting from the body, missing the jerk forward, falling backward in the
snatch, hyperflexing in the squat) as plausible, mechanistically-grounded coaching
heuristics rather than quantified, tested probabilities. It also does not address every
lift pattern (bench press cervical hyperextension is mentioned only briefly, in the
adjoining text) with the same depth as the Olympic-lift-family discussion.

**Example** — A lifter who habitually looks up and back during the snatch's overhead squat
receiving position, and repeatedly loses the lift backward, is exhibiting exactly the
failure mode this section attributes to premature backward head tilt — the fix is a fixed,
forward-and-slightly-down gaze target, not simply "sit up straighter."

subsection's pelvis-and-lumbar-safety discussion, same overall posture section);

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate — coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed pp. 155-156, "3.3.4.4

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes, and that isokinetic
symmetry testing measures an isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent
functional, whole-movement asymmetry accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply — direct tension with current Baylor practice.** This claim sits in
real tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection
model explicitly includes symmetry (L/R differences) as an optional force-plate reporting
category (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and force-plate/isokinetic symmetry indices are in active use for
rehab and return-to-play decisions. **Eric's review would be needed** to reconcile this
1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based "correction" with the department's
modern use of symmetry metrics; this entry does not resolve that tension, it only flags it
— the book's objection is specifically to *using an isokinetic ratio to drive a
correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry monitoring for RTP tracking purposes
more broadly, but Eric's own view on where that line falls is not stated anywhere in the
corpus reviewed for `method-baseline.md`.

athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not automatically
something to "fix" — the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a natural,
individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

name) whenever normalizing strength testing data across athletes of different
bodymass — e.g. comparing back-squat 1RM across a football roster spanning 180-320+ lb
linemen to skill players is misleading without some bodymass adjustment, and simple
per-kg relative strength (load/bodymass) is itself an approximation that over- or
under-corrects depending where an athlete sits on this curve. **Eric's baseline:** relevant
to the department's stated need for sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data (currently
a named gap per `performance-playbook-development-plan.md` 3.2.3) — a bodymass-adjusted
strength-comparison method, even a simplified version of Siff's approach, would be a
concrete way to build fairer cross-position strength benchmarks for football specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific numeric constants (a, b, c values) are fit to
weightlifting and powerlifting records through 1987-1988 and to Russian weightlifter height
data of that era — they should not be applied directly to football or other sport
populations without refitting to relevant data. The dimensional-analysis argument for the
two-thirds exponent is general reasoning the authors give, but Lietzke's best-fit exponent
(0.6748) and Siff's regression constants are single-dataset fits; the "60-67 kg
relative-strength peak" finding is specific to Olympic/power lifters of that period and
should be treated as illustrative, not directly transferable without refitting.

**Example** — Comparing a 90 kg lifter's 405 kg powerlifting total to a 140 kg lifter's 500
kg total by raw numbers alone favors the heavier lifter; converting each to a percentage of
the world-class total expected at their own bodymass (via Table 3.3's fitted curve) gives a
fairer relative-strength comparison, which is the entire point of this scaling approach.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations]] (the next
subsection's parallel age-adjustment method, explicitly combined with this bodymass
adjustment in the book's own worked example); [[claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass]]
(uses the same bodymass-normalization logic for sex comparison).

######## claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.3.7"
topic: strength across the lifespan
category: [strength, testing, age]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Strength Peaks at 20-28, Declines ~1%/Year After 30 — And Lab vs. Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year. The text compares two measurement approaches:
laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al 1961; MacDougall et al
1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across juvenile, junior, senior, and
Masters (40+) age-group records. The two datasets agree reasonably well through adolescence
but diverge at the extremes: lab measurements score prepubescent lifters *higher* than
competition data would suggest (attributed to weight-trained children being much stronger
than untrained peers of the same age, biasing the comparison), and lab measurements score
older lifters (55+) *higher* than their competition performance, attributed to Olympic
weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across multiple muscle groups,
versus dynamometer testing of one isolated muscle group (usually quadriceps). Linear
regression fits the 30-80 age decline for each dataset: for untrained lab subjects, %S =
120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S = 140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996),
where A is age in years — the steeper slope for trained lifters implies *more* absolute
decline per year for those who had reached a higher peak, even though both groups decline
by roughly the same fraction. A worked example combines this with the bodymass-adjustment
equations (3.3.5) to show a 45-year-old, 80 kg lifter with a 260 kg total (87.1%
age-and-bodymass-adjusted score) can have *greater* relative strength than a young 90 kg
lifter with a 350 kg total (86.3% bodymass-adjusted, no age adjustment needed) — illustrating
that raw totals alone can mask true relative-strength standing across ages. (PDF pp.
170-173, printed pp. 159-162, "3.3.7 The Relationship between Strength and Age,"
Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline
itself (that is well-documented broadly in exercise-science, e.g. sarcopenia); the
explanation offered here is specifically for *why the two measurement methods disagree* at
the young and old extremes — differing skill/technical demands (isolated-joint dynamometer
testing vs. whole-body competitive lifting) mean the two methods are not measuring
identical constructs, especially where technical skill and multi-joint coordination (more
present in older, more experienced competitive lifters, and more absent in
still-developing young lifters) partially compensates for or masks the underlying raw
strength trend.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer/force-plate
testing is likely to be a fairer read on very young or very old populations than
competition-style multi-joint lift performance, which conflates raw strength with
accumulated technical skill. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen
through fifth-year seniors), this suggests raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift itself differs systematically
by experience/class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific regression equations are fit to weightlifting records
and a small number of lab studies (Hettinger 1961; MacDougall 1982) predating this text's
publication; the exact numeric coefficients (120.17, 0.68865, 140.15, 1.3853) should be
treated as illustrative of that era's data and that specific population, not as a precise,
individually-applicable age-adjustment formula for a current athlete population. This entry
does not claim the underlying decline pattern is independently confirmed beyond these
cited sources; no other source is named here to corroborate it.

**Example** — Comparing a 22-year-old's and a 45-year-old assistant coach's back squat by
raw weight alone (or even bodymass-adjusted alone) undercounts the older lifter's relative
standing; applying both the bodymass adjustment (3.3.5) and the age adjustment (equation
3.9) together, as the book's own worked example does, can reverse which lifter actually has
the higher relative strength.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the paired bodymass-adjustment
method this age adjustment is explicitly combined with).
######## claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass.md
---
type: library-entry

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases** — 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7) — meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, and hip flexors/extensors and knee
flexors/masticating muscles tied at 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any groups tested;
verified directly against the PDF page image, since the raw text-extraction JSON had
mis-rendered the knee-flexors/masticating-muscles value as 0.60). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed pp.
161-162, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven mainly by
*how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any difference
in muscle tissue quality. **Inference:** the text separately notes the muscle-group ratios
"probably" reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between average men and women,
but it does not itself connect that habitual-use explanation to the specific pattern of
which muscle groups show the largest and smallest sex gaps (elbow flexors/extensors lowest
at 0.55, hip flexors/extensors highest at 0.80); that specific connection is this entry's
own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make sentence-by-sentence.

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes — the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline:** relevant
context for the department's existing choice to default women's-sport strength testing to
repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing week1-lecture.md p.39) — this table gives a physiological rationale for why a single
sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across different lifts/muscle groups if the
department ever wanted to build sex-specific relative-strength benchmarks by exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously —
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — Using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every exercise would
overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there (0.55) and
underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap (0.80), per
Table 3.8.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).
######## claim--secular-increase-in-lifting-performance-gompertz-growth.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

category: [strength, historical-trend, doping]

---

# Elite Lifting Performance Rose Steadily by Decade (Gompertz Curve); the Press's Faster Growth May Reflect Steroid Use

**What it is** — Normalizing weightlifting performance across all bodymass divisions (as a
percentage of the mean of the ten heaviest totals ever recorded per division, via the
bodymass-scaling equation from 3.3.5) and plotting the result by year from 1950-1990 shows a
**Gompertz growth curve** (Points y = a.e^(-b.e^(-cx)), x = year-1950) fits the historical
rise in performance well for the snatch, clean-and-jerk, and press (R = 0.994-0.996 for
each, with separate fitted constants a, b, c per lift). The snatch and clean-and-jerk show a
similar growth trend, but the **press grew measurably faster**. Since the Olympic press was
removed from competition in 1971, its longer-term trend cannot be studied further. (PDF pp.
172-173, printed pp. 161-162, "3.3.9 The Increase in Human Strength over Time," Fig 3.26.)

**Why it works** — The Gompertz form itself is a standard actuarial/biological growth-curve
choice for processes with an early accelerating phase followed by a plateau approaching some
ceiling — it fits generic athletic-record progression patterns generally, not something
specific to strength physiology. For the *differential* growth rate between lifts, the text
offers an explicitly labeled interpretation, not a proven mechanism: Siff and Medvedev
"have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic
substances since the late 1950s," reasoning that the press is slower, more
quasi-isometric, and more dependent on muscle hypertrophy and relative strength than the
more technically-demanding snatch and clean-and-jerk, and that anabolic substances would be
expected to preferentially benefit hypertrophy-dependent, technically-simpler lifts (also
naming the powerlifting squat, bench press, and deadlift as lifts that would be expected to
benefit similarly).

**When to apply** — The Gompertz-curve secular-trend finding itself is useful background for
understanding why raw historical strength-record comparisons across decades are misleading
without normalizing for era; the steroid explanation should be treated and cited
specifically as the authors' own **speculative interpretation** of a correlational pattern
(different growth rates for different lifts), not as an established causal finding.

**When NOT to apply** — The steroid-use explanation is explicitly hedged by the authors
themselves ("it is reasonable to expect...") and is not a tested causal claim — no doping
prevalence data, testing records, or controlled comparison is presented to support it
directly; it should be reported as the authors' own inference from an indirect pattern
(differential growth rates by lift type), never as a confirmed finding. The Gompertz fit
itself is also a single dataset ending in 1990 and should not be extrapolated to predict
current-era performance ceilings without updated data.

**Example** — Citing "weightlifting has improved steadily since 1950 per a Gompertz growth
model" is a supportable, quantified historical claim; citing "the press grew faster because
of steroids" as an established fact (rather than "Siff and Medvedev's own hypothesis, based
on the press's lower technical demand") would overstate what this section actually shows.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the same normalization method
used to build this secular-trend dataset).
######## framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.4.1"
topic: warm-up mechanism and prescription
category: [warm-up, programming, coaching]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Warm-Up Works Through Temperature and CNS Priming, and Its Value Is Event- and Training-Status-Specific

**What it is** — The warm-up has two components: **general** (raising the body's overall
functional potential) and **specific** (establishing the optimal relationship between the
CNS and the upcoming movement). The text argues "warm-up" is a misleading name, since the
CNS-priming role can matter more than literal tissue warming, and proposes "pre-activity
preparation" as a more accurate term, covering neural priming, physical tissue warming, and
psychological readying. **Temperature mechanism**: muscle contracts faster and more
intensely as temperature rises within a safe range, and electrical muscle activity rises
with body temperature (Golenhofen & Goptert 1958; Book & Golenhofen 1959); a hot shower
increases isometric endurance and cyclic-work speed/endurance by 7.5-9.0%; cooling to 18°C
shortens muscular work capacity 2-3x; massage does not change cyclic endurance but does
increase explosive-work power. **Activity-specific evidence**: active, intense warm-ups
(not moderate-intensity ones) effectively prepare for speed-strength/explosive work,
producing measured gains such as +1.0-4.5 cm in women's basketball jumps, up to +10 cm in
long jump, +400-700 N boxing punch force with 0.02-0.04 s faster striking time, and
correlation between rest interval and punch force rising from R=0.40 (no warm-up) to
R=0.62 (after warm-up). Franks' literature summary (cited via Williams, 1983) gives the
governing decision rules: high-intensity short-duration events (weightlifting, shotput)
benefit from warming up; vigorous warm-up can *hurt* endurance-sport performance; low-intensity/endurance
athletes gain little from warming up; direct warm-ups (task-similar activity) at moderate
intensity/duration help trained athletes in explosive sports but not necessarily untrained
ones; indirect warm-ups (unrelated activity, e.g. cycling, stretching) can help if kept
unstressful; nearly all studies showing warm-up as *detrimental* used untrained subjects
who could not tolerate high-intensity warm-ups; and strenuous, non-specific warm-ups can
interfere with motor-skill-dependent sports. (PDF pp. 173-176, printed pp. 162-165,
"3.4 Factors Increasing the Working Effect of Strength," "3.4.1 The Warm-up and
Pre-Activity Preparation.")

**Why it works** — Temperature effects act at the muscle-fibre level (contraction speed and
force rise with safe-range temperature increases, and post-stimulation active-state
duration shortens with heat); the CNS-priming component works by establishing task-specific
neural readiness before the main effort, which is why "little or no general physical
warming up may be necessary" for sports (Olympic lifting, gymnastics) whose competitive
movements themselves double as adequate specific preparation, and why endurance events
(marathon) need essentially no dedicated specific warm-up since the event itself provides it.

**When to apply** — Use the Franks decision rules directly when designing warm-up protocols
by sport/session type: prescribe active, direct (task-similar), moderate-to-high-intensity
warm-ups before explosive/power/max-strength work for trained athletes specifically, and
favor lighter, indirect warm-ups (or none) before pure endurance work. **Eric's baseline:**
directly usable to formalize warm-up prescription language in Baylor's own S&C
programming and in the HHPR 5355 curriculum material, since the department's documented
practice does not currently specify a warm-up decision framework distinct from general
programming guidance.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific performance-gain numbers (jump height, punch force,
strike time) are single old studies on specific populations (women's basketball, boxers,
long jumpers) and should be treated as illustrative magnitude, not as guaranteed or
individually-applicable gains. The Franks rules are themselves a literature summary from
1983 sources, not a fresh meta-analysis; they capture broad, still-plausible patterns but
should be applied as heuristics, not fixed thresholds.

**Example** — Prescribing a long, generalized, non-specific dynamic warm-up before a
football lineman's max-effort squat testing session risks the "strenuous, non-specific
warm-up interferes with skill" failure mode per Franks; a shorter, direct (squat-pattern-specific)
warm-up ramping intensity toward the working weight better fits this framework's guidance
for trained athletes in an explosive/max-strength task.

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
immediately following subsection, on how a *specific prior strength stimulus* — not just a
general warm-up — further boosts subsequent performance).
######## claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.4.2"
topic: contested evidence for post-activation potentiation
category: [potentiation, testing, contested-evidence]
confidence: contested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Whether a Prior Heavy Stimulus Reliably Boosts Subsequent Performance Is Genuinely Contested Across the Cited Literature

**What it is** — The text explicitly flags that "research into the after-effects of
muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature." Cited findings on
both sides, within the same short passage: a statistically significant increase in
unloaded-movement speed directly after the same movement performed with added weight
(Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962) — but other research found **no such effect**, despite
subjective athlete reports that movements "felt quicker" after using loads (Nofsinger,
1963; Nelson & Lambert, 1965); no measurable increase in vertical jump shortly after
preceding resistive exercise (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965); and shot-put results that actually
**deteriorated** after preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
By contrast, the Russian-literature studies detailed in
[[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961;
Diachkov 1961 and others) consistently report positive potentiation effects with specific
load, timing, and sequencing parameters. The text does not reconcile these two literatures
or explain the discrepancy. (PDF p. 176, printed p. 164-165, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of
Muscle Activity.")

**Why it works** — No mechanism for the disagreement is offered by the authors.
**Inference:** plausible contributors (not stated in the text) could include differences in
the specific loads, rest intervals, and movements tested across studies, differences in
subject training status, or measurement sensitivity — but since the book itself does not
investigate or resolve this, any explanation beyond "the cited Western and Russian studies
disagree" would be unsupported speculation.

**When to apply** — Cite this contested status explicitly whenever presenting
post-activation-potentiation research to Baylor staff: the specific, quantified
prescriptions in [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] come
from the Russian side of a literature that, by this book's own account, does not uniformly
agree the phenomenon shows up as measured, even for broadly similar movements (jumps,
throws). This matters directly for how confidently a PAP/complex-training protocol should
be presented to coaches as "evidence-based."

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat this contested framing as evidence that PAP "doesn't
work" — the disagreement runs in the specific direction of some Western studies finding no
effect or a negative effect under their own testing conditions, not a general finding that
potentiation never occurs; nor should it be read as proof the Russian findings are simply
correct and the Western ones flawed. The most honest reading, per the brief's rule against
harmonizing conflicting sources, is that the *net direction and reliability* of PAP under
any specific protocol needs verification with the department's own athletes and equipment
before being trusted as a general effect.

**Example** — If a Baylor coach cites "post-activation potentiation reliably boosts vertical
jump" as settled science, this entry is the citable correction: even within this one book's
own review of the (dated) literature, at least one cited study found no jump-height increase
at all after a resistive-exercise stimulus (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965), and another found a
throwing event's performance got worse (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
Russian-literature-based prescription this claim directly qualifies).
######## framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.4.2"
topic: post-activation potentiation prescription
category: [potentiation, programming, testing]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Post-Tetanic (Post-Activation) Potentiation: Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

**What it is** — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent
activity is measurably altered — a phenomenon called (in Western physiology) post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters** — preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric) does not show the
same improvement; the effect appears from the very first subsequent contraction (with a
residual inhibitory trace on the first rep) and strengthens sharply by the second
contraction. **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest post-isometric
dynamic-strength boost (90%) came after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7%
boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8% — "the optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for
obtaining the greatest post-work improvement" — though with rising fitness, larger loads
(up to 100% max) can start producing the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing
window** depends on the conditioning stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive
isometric force rose 25% within the first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5
minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped 2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for
vertical jump specifically, barbell squats potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes
post, while depth jumps potentiated jump height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes
post. Higher-load isometric stimuli (100% 1RM) took *longest* to reach peak potentiation
(15.4 min) versus 50% 1RM (17.2 min, longest) versus 25% 1RM (12 min, fastest) in one
dataset (Ilin, 1961) — so the load-to-timing relationship is not perfectly monotonic
across every study cited. **Rest interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not
(Klimonov, 1965). **Delayed effects**: moderate-volume barbell work produces a positive
tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect
by 5-6 days. (PDF pp. 175-178, printed pp. 164-166, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle
Activity," Figs 3.27-3.29.)

**Why it works** — The text frames this as a nervous-system "after-effect" or "trace"
phenomenon: any stimulus, momentary or not, leaves a lingering trace in the nervous system
reflecting its relative inertness, which is proposed as foundational to how fitness
continues rising despite periodic breaks in training. The text also separately states that
heavy dynamic work "elicits a positive after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS),
which produces a general toning influence on the motor apparatus." **Inference:** treating
the isometric-then-dynamic sequencing effect specifically as an instance of this same
central-trace/CNS-toning mechanism, rather than a purely local muscular effect, connects
two statements the text makes separately; the authors do not state this connection in one
sentence.

**When to apply** — Use this as a concrete, quantified starting template for complex/contrast
training design (heavy strength stimulus paired with an explosive movement): favor ~50% 1RM
isometric or heavy-tonic conditioning stimuli over maximal loads for athletes not yet highly
trained; expect the potentiation window to open within 1 minute and build over several
minutes, with the peak timing shifting later (toward 8-10 minutes) for a more demanding
stimulus like depth jumps versus barbell squats; and program the explosive/dynamic movement
*after* the conditioning stimulus, never the reverse order, per the sequencing finding.
**Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this offers a citable, historically-grounded
starting point (a squat-then-jump contrast pair with a 3-5 minute rest window) if the
department wants to formalize a PAP/complex-training protocol, to be validated against the
department's own force-plate (CMJ) data on actual athletes before being adopted as policy.

**When NOT to apply** — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies
(Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg
extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as
non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this
should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This
framework should be read alongside [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]],
which documents that Western studies of the same general phenomenon found much weaker or
absent effects — the sequencing/timing rules here reflect the Russian dataset specifically,
not a universally-replicated finding.

**Example** — A contrast-training set of back squats at ~50-60% 1RM followed 3-4 minutes
later by depth jumps (or vice versa, testing depth-jump-first conditioning with an 8-10
minute wait before the explosive test movement) is a direct, testable application of this
framework's load and timing findings for a Baylor athlete.

**Related** — [[framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines]] (the preceding
subsection on general warm-up, a related but distinct CNS-priming phenomenon);
[[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]] (the documented Western/Russian

# Strength Peaks at 20-28, Declines ~1%/Year After 30 — And Lab vs. Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year. The text compares two measurement approaches:
laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al 1961; MacDougall et al
1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across juvenile, junior, senior, and
Masters (40+) age-group records. The two datasets agree reasonably well through adolescence
but diverge at the extremes: lab measurements score prepubescent lifters *higher* than
competition data would suggest (attributed to weight-trained children being much stronger
than untrained peers of the same age, biasing the comparison), and lab measurements score
older lifters (55+) *higher* than their competition performance, attributed to Olympic
weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across multiple muscle groups,
versus dynamometer testing of one isolated muscle group (usually quadriceps). Linear
regression fits the 30-80 age decline for each dataset: for untrained lab subjects, %S =
120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S = 140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996),
where A is age in years — the steeper slope for trained lifters implies *more* absolute
decline per year for those who had reached a higher peak, even though both groups decline
by roughly the same fraction. A worked example combines this with the bodymass-adjustment
equations (3.3.5) to show a 45-year-old, 80 kg lifter with a 260 kg total (87.1%
age-and-bodymass-adjusted score) can have *greater* relative strength than a young 90 kg
lifter with a 350 kg total (86.3% bodymass-adjusted, no age adjustment needed) — illustrating
that raw totals alone can mask true relative-strength standing across ages. (PDF pp.
170-173, printed pp. 159-162, "3.3.7 The Relationship between Strength and Age,"
Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline
itself (that is well-documented broadly in exercise-science, e.g. sarcopenia); the
explanation offered here is specifically for *why the two measurement methods disagree* at
the young and old extremes — differing skill/technical demands (isolated-joint dynamometer
testing vs. whole-body competitive lifting) mean the two methods are not measuring
identical constructs, especially where technical skill and multi-joint coordination (more
present in older, more experienced competitive lifters, and more absent in
still-developing young lifters) partially compensates for or masks the underlying raw
strength trend.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer/force-plate
testing is likely to be a fairer read on very young or very old populations than
competition-style multi-joint lift performance, which conflates raw strength with
accumulated technical skill. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen
through fifth-year seniors), this suggests raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift itself differs systematically
by experience/class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific regression equations are fit to weightlifting records
and a small number of lab studies (Hettinger 1961; MacDougall 1982) predating this text's
publication; the exact numeric coefficients (120.17, 0.68865, 140.15, 1.3853) should be
treated as illustrative of that era's data and that specific population, not as a precise,
individually-applicable age-adjustment formula for a current athlete population. This entry
does not claim the underlying decline pattern is independently confirmed beyond these
cited sources; no other source is named here to corroborate it.

**Example** — Comparing a 22-year-old's and a 45-year-old assistant coach's back squat by
raw weight alone (or even bodymass-adjusted alone) undercounts the older lifter's relative
standing; applying both the bodymass adjustment (3.3.5) and the age adjustment (equation
3.9) together, as the book's own worked example does, can reverse which lifter actually has
the higher relative strength.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the paired bodymass-adjustment
method this age adjustment is explicitly combined with).

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases** — 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7) — meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, and hip flexors/extensors and knee
flexors/masticating muscles tied at 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any groups tested;
verified directly against the PDF page image, since the raw text-extraction JSON had
mis-rendered the knee-flexors/masticating-muscles value as 0.60). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed pp.
161-162, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven mainly by
*how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any difference
in muscle tissue quality. **Inference:** the text separately notes the muscle-group ratios
"probably" reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between average men and women,
but it does not itself connect that habitual-use explanation to the specific pattern of
which muscle groups show the largest and smallest sex gaps (elbow flexors/extensors lowest
at 0.55, hip flexors/extensors highest at 0.80); that specific connection is this entry's
own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make sentence-by-sentence.

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes — the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline:** relevant
context for the department's existing choice to default women's-sport strength testing to
repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing week1-lecture.md p.39) — this table gives a physiological rationale for why a single
sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across different lifts/muscle groups if the
department ever wanted to build sex-specific relative-strength benchmarks by exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously —
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — Using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every exercise would
overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there (0.55) and
underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap (0.80), per
Table 3.8.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).

# Elite Lifting Performance Rose Steadily by Decade (Gompertz Curve); the Press's Faster Growth May Reflect Steroid Use

**What it is** — Normalizing weightlifting performance across all bodymass divisions (as a
percentage of the mean of the ten heaviest totals ever recorded per division, via the
bodymass-scaling equation from 3.3.5) and plotting the result by year from 1950-1990 shows a
**Gompertz growth curve** (Points y = a.e^(-b.e^(-cx)), x = year-1950) fits the historical
rise in performance well for the snatch, clean-and-jerk, and press (R = 0.994-0.996 for
each, with separate fitted constants a, b, c per lift). The snatch and clean-and-jerk show a
similar growth trend, but the **press grew measurably faster**. Since the Olympic press was
removed from competition in 1971, its longer-term trend cannot be studied further. (PDF pp.
172-173, printed pp. 161-162, "3.3.9 The Increase in Human Strength over Time," Fig 3.26.)

**Why it works** — The Gompertz form itself is a standard actuarial/biological growth-curve
choice for processes with an early accelerating phase followed by a plateau approaching some
ceiling — it fits generic athletic-record progression patterns generally, not something
specific to strength physiology. For the *differential* growth rate between lifts, the text
offers an explicitly labeled interpretation, not a proven mechanism: Siff and Medvedev
"have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic
substances since the late 1950s," reasoning that the press is slower, more
quasi-isometric, and more dependent on muscle hypertrophy and relative strength than the
more technically-demanding snatch and clean-and-jerk, and that anabolic substances would be
expected to preferentially benefit hypertrophy-dependent, technically-simpler lifts (also
naming the powerlifting squat, bench press, and deadlift as lifts that would be expected to
benefit similarly).

**When to apply** — The Gompertz-curve secular-trend finding itself is useful background for
understanding why raw historical strength-record comparisons across decades are misleading
without normalizing for era; the steroid explanation should be treated and cited
specifically as the authors' own **speculative interpretation** of a correlational pattern
(different growth rates for different lifts), not as an established causal finding.

**When NOT to apply** — The steroid-use explanation is explicitly hedged by the authors
themselves ("it is reasonable to expect...") and is not a tested causal claim — no doping
prevalence data, testing records, or controlled comparison is presented to support it
directly; it should be reported as the authors' own inference from an indirect pattern
(differential growth rates by lift type), never as a confirmed finding. The Gompertz fit
itself is also a single dataset ending in 1990 and should not be extrapolated to predict
current-era performance ceilings without updated data.

**Example** — Citing "weightlifting has improved steadily since 1950 per a Gompertz growth
model" is a supportable, quantified historical claim; citing "the press grew faster because
of steroids" as an established fact (rather than "Siff and Medvedev's own hypothesis, based
on the press's lower technical demand") would overstate what this section actually shows.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the same normalization method
used to build this secular-trend dataset).

# Warm-Up Works Through Temperature and CNS Priming, and Its Value Is Event- and Training-Status-Specific

**What it is** — The warm-up has two components: **general** (raising the body's overall
functional potential) and **specific** (establishing the optimal relationship between the
CNS and the upcoming movement). The text argues "warm-up" is a misleading name, since the
CNS-priming role can matter more than literal tissue warming, and proposes "pre-activity
preparation" as a more accurate term, covering neural priming, physical tissue warming, and
psychological readying. **Temperature mechanism**: muscle contracts faster and more
intensely as temperature rises within a safe range, and electrical muscle activity rises
with body temperature (Golenhofen & Goptert 1958; Book & Golenhofen 1959); a hot shower
increases isometric endurance and cyclic-work speed/endurance by 7.5-9.0%; cooling to 18°C
shortens muscular work capacity 2-3x; massage does not change cyclic endurance but does
increase explosive-work power. **Activity-specific evidence**: active, intense warm-ups
(not moderate-intensity ones) effectively prepare for speed-strength/explosive work,
producing measured gains such as +1.0-4.5 cm in women's basketball jumps, up to +10 cm in
long jump, +400-700 N boxing punch force with 0.02-0.04 s faster striking time, and
correlation between rest interval and punch force rising from R=0.40 (no warm-up) to
R=0.62 (after warm-up). Franks' literature summary (cited via Williams, 1983) gives the
governing decision rules: high-intensity short-duration events (weightlifting, shotput)
benefit from warming up; vigorous warm-up can *hurt* endurance-sport performance; low-intensity/endurance
athletes gain little from warming up; direct warm-ups (task-similar activity) at moderate
intensity/duration help trained athletes in explosive sports but not necessarily untrained
ones; indirect warm-ups (unrelated activity, e.g. cycling, stretching) can help if kept
unstressful; nearly all studies showing warm-up as *detrimental* used untrained subjects
who could not tolerate high-intensity warm-ups; and strenuous, non-specific warm-ups can
interfere with motor-skill-dependent sports. (PDF pp. 173-176, printed pp. 162-165,
"3.4 Factors Increasing the Working Effect of Strength," "3.4.1 The Warm-up and
Pre-Activity Preparation.")

**Why it works** — Temperature effects act at the muscle-fibre level (contraction speed and
force rise with safe-range temperature increases, and post-stimulation active-state
duration shortens with heat); the CNS-priming component works by establishing task-specific
neural readiness before the main effort, which is why "little or no general physical
warming up may be necessary" for sports (Olympic lifting, gymnastics) whose competitive
movements themselves double as adequate specific preparation, and why endurance events
(marathon) need essentially no dedicated specific warm-up since the event itself provides it.

**When to apply** — Use the Franks decision rules directly when designing warm-up protocols
by sport/session type: prescribe active, direct (task-similar), moderate-to-high-intensity
warm-ups before explosive/power/max-strength work for trained athletes specifically, and
favor lighter, indirect warm-ups (or none) before pure endurance work. **Eric's baseline:**
directly usable to formalize warm-up prescription language in Baylor's own S&C
programming and in the HHPR 5355 curriculum material, since the department's documented
practice does not currently specify a warm-up decision framework distinct from general
programming guidance.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific performance-gain numbers (jump height, punch force,
strike time) are single old studies on specific populations (women's basketball, boxers,
long jumpers) and should be treated as illustrative magnitude, not as guaranteed or
individually-applicable gains. The Franks rules are themselves a literature summary from
1983 sources, not a fresh meta-analysis; they capture broad, still-plausible patterns but
should be applied as heuristics, not fixed thresholds.

**Example** — Prescribing a long, generalized, non-specific dynamic warm-up before a
football lineman's max-effort squat testing session risks the "strenuous, non-specific
warm-up interferes with skill" failure mode per Franks; a shorter, direct (squat-pattern-specific)
warm-up ramping intensity toward the working weight better fits this framework's guidance
for trained athletes in an explosive/max-strength task.

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
immediately following subsection, on how a *specific prior strength stimulus* — not just a
general warm-up — further boosts subsequent performance).

# Whether a Prior Heavy Stimulus Reliably Boosts Subsequent Performance Is Genuinely Contested Across the Cited Literature

**What it is** — The text explicitly flags that "research into the after-effects of
muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature." Cited findings on
both sides, within the same short passage: a statistically significant increase in
unloaded-movement speed directly after the same movement performed with added weight
(Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962) — but other research found **no such effect**, despite
subjective athlete reports that movements "felt quicker" after using loads (Nofsinger,
1963; Nelson & Lambert, 1965); no measurable increase in vertical jump shortly after
preceding resistive exercise (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965); and shot-put results that actually
**deteriorated** after preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
By contrast, the Russian-literature studies detailed in
[[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961;
Diachkov 1961 and others) consistently report positive potentiation effects with specific
load, timing, and sequencing parameters. The text does not reconcile these two literatures
or explain the discrepancy. (PDF p. 176, printed p. 164-165, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of
Muscle Activity.")

**Why it works** — No mechanism for the disagreement is offered by the authors.
**Inference:** plausible contributors (not stated in the text) could include differences in
the specific loads, rest intervals, and movements tested across studies, differences in
subject training status, or measurement sensitivity — but since the book itself does not
investigate or resolve this, any explanation beyond "the cited Western and Russian studies
disagree" would be unsupported speculation.

**When to apply** — Cite this contested status explicitly whenever presenting
post-activation-potentiation research to Baylor staff: the specific, quantified
prescriptions in [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] come
from the Russian side of a literature that, by this book's own account, does not uniformly
agree the phenomenon shows up as measured, even for broadly similar movements (jumps,
throws). This matters directly for how confidently a PAP/complex-training protocol should
be presented to coaches as "evidence-based."

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat this contested framing as evidence that PAP "doesn't
work" — the disagreement runs in the specific direction of some Western studies finding no
effect or a negative effect under their own testing conditions, not a general finding that
potentiation never occurs; nor should it be read as proof the Russian findings are simply
correct and the Western ones flawed. The most honest reading, per the brief's rule against
harmonizing conflicting sources, is that the *net direction and reliability* of PAP under
any specific protocol needs verification with the department's own athletes and equipment
before being trusted as a general effect.

**Example** — If a Baylor coach cites "post-activation potentiation reliably boosts vertical
jump" as settled science, this entry is the citable correction: even within this one book's
own review of the (dated) literature, at least one cited study found no jump-height increase
at all after a resistive-exercise stimulus (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965), and another found a
throwing event's performance got worse (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
Russian-literature-based prescription this claim directly qualifies).

# Post-Tetanic (Post-Activation) Potentiation: Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

**What it is** — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent
activity is measurably altered — a phenomenon called (in Western physiology) post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters** — preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric) does not show the
same improvement; the effect appears from the very first subsequent contraction (with a
residual inhibitory trace on the first rep) and strengthens sharply by the second
contraction. **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest post-isometric
dynamic-strength boost (90%) came after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7%
boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8% — "the optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for
obtaining the greatest post-work improvement" — though with rising fitness, larger loads
(up to 100% max) can start producing the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing
window** depends on the conditioning stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive
isometric force rose 25% within the first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5
minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped 2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for
vertical jump specifically, barbell squats potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes
post, while depth jumps potentiated jump height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes
post. Higher-load isometric stimuli (100% 1RM) took *longest* to reach peak potentiation
(15.4 min) versus 50% 1RM (17.2 min, longest) versus 25% 1RM (12 min, fastest) in one
dataset (Ilin, 1961) — so the load-to-timing relationship is not perfectly monotonic
across every study cited. **Rest interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not
(Klimonov, 1965). **Delayed effects**: moderate-volume barbell work produces a positive
tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect
by 5-6 days. (PDF pp. 175-178, printed pp. 164-166, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle
Activity," Figs 3.27-3.29.)

**Why it works** — The text frames this as a nervous-system "after-effect" or "trace"
phenomenon: any stimulus, momentary or not, leaves a lingering trace in the nervous system
reflecting its relative inertness, which is proposed as foundational to how fitness
continues rising despite periodic breaks in training. The text also separately states that
heavy dynamic work "elicits a positive after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS),
which produces a general toning influence on the motor apparatus." **Inference:** treating
the isometric-then-dynamic sequencing effect specifically as an instance of this same
central-trace/CNS-toning mechanism, rather than a purely local muscular effect, connects
two statements the text makes separately; the authors do not state this connection in one
sentence.

**When to apply** — Use this as a concrete, quantified starting template for complex/contrast
training design (heavy strength stimulus paired with an explosive movement): favor ~50% 1RM
isometric or heavy-tonic conditioning stimuli over maximal loads for athletes not yet highly
trained; expect the potentiation window to open within 1 minute and build over several
minutes, with the peak timing shifting later (toward 8-10 minutes) for a more demanding
stimulus like depth jumps versus barbell squats; and program the explosive/dynamic movement
*after* the conditioning stimulus, never the reverse order, per the sequencing finding.
**Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this offers a citable, historically-grounded
starting point (a squat-then-jump contrast pair with a 3-5 minute rest window) if the
department wants to formalize a PAP/complex-training protocol, to be validated against the
department's own force-plate (CMJ) data on actual athletes before being adopted as policy.

**When NOT to apply** — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies
(Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg
extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as
non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this
should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This
framework should be read alongside [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]],
which documents that Western studies of the same general phenomenon found much weaker or
absent effects — the sequencing/timing rules here reflect the Russian dataset specifically,
not a universally-replicated finding.

**Example** — A contrast-training set of back squats at ~50-60% 1RM followed 3-4 minutes
later by depth jumps (or vice versa, testing depth-jump-first conditioning with an 8-10
minute wait before the explosive test movement) is a direct, testable application of this
framework's load and timing findings for a Baylor athlete.

**Related** — [[framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines]] (the preceding
subsection on general warm-up, a related but distinct CNS-priming phenomenon);
[[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]] (the documented Western/Russian
disagreement on whether this effect reliably occurs at all).

-long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
-capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
-strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural

-motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
-reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
-enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
-patterns that decay quickly without continued training.
+**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
+lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
+muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
+maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
+enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
+printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
+enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
+1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
+phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
+(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
+p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
+quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
+kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
-**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
-enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
-because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
-more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
-experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
-rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
-run on the same subjects who produced the durations.
+**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
+aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
+"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum

# Narrow-Stance Quarter Squats Transfer Better to Sprinting Than Wide Squats

**What it is** — Moyer's worked example of "it depends" in the strength-vs-speed debate: "studies have shown that quarter squatting with a narrow stance transfers better to speed and jumping than does wide squatting." He does not drop full or wide squatting. Lower-level athletes still get general transfer from it. But **as competition approaches, his squatting becomes narrower and shallower**, moving toward a quarter squat. The same partial-range logic runs through his special-strength choices: Yessis delay squats go only to about quarter depth.

**Why it works** — Two mechanisms are implied. Neither is demonstrated in the course. (1) Identical elements: a narrow, shallow squat is closer to sprint stance-leg joint angles and foot position. (2) Accentuation ([[heuristic--accentuation-band-setup-knee-drive-pawback-sprint]]): train strength where the sport needs peak force, not across a full range the sprint never uses.

**When to apply** — Late off-season and in-season blocks for skill players, where the goal is converting strength to speed with limited time. A heavy quarter squat or partial-range isometric can be a low-fatigue, sprint-angle strength dose.

**When NOT to apply** — Moyer names no study. There is a partial-vs-full squat literature, but its transfer results are mixed and it was not checked for this entry. Treat "transfers better" as unverified. Partial squats let athletes handle very large loads, which brings spinal-load and technique-drift risk for heavy linemen. Full-range work still has hypertrophy and joint-range value that a quarter squat does not replace, especially after injury, when restoring full knee and hip range is a rehab goal in its own right. The stance-width claim may not apply to positions whose sport stance is wi

**Example** — Big 12 in-season Tuesday for WR/DB: replace the back squat to parallel with a narrow-stance quarter squat for 3×3, plus a delay-squat isometric. Keep the full-depth squat in the linemen's program and in the summer block.

**Related** — [[claim--exercise-selection-over-intensity-volume-sprint]] — same logic: pick the variant with more shared elements.

# The Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas

**What it is** — Moyer's map of whose ideas sit under current speed and strength practice. Use it to **trace a modern concept back to its source** before judging it.

| Figure | What Moyer credits them with | Where it shows up now |
|---|---|---|
| **Lev Matveyev** | *Fundamentals of Sports Training* (Russian 1965, English c. 1981); **general vs. specific training** | Linear periodization; the general/special exercise split |
| **Vladimir Zatsiorsky** | Soviet school of biomechanics; *Science and Practice of Strength Training*; later Penn State | Hip-flexor range and sprint biomechanics data Moyer cites |
| **Atko Viru** | Endocrine and metabolic adaptation to training; *Adaptation in Sports Training* | Training monitoring |
| **Anatoliy Bondarchuk** | Hammer champion and throws coach; **transfer of training** from correlational data on thousands of athletes | Exercise classification by transfer |
| **Yuri Verkhoshansky** | Shock method (plyometrics), special strength, block training, **dynamic correspondence** and **key movements** | Special-strength exercise design |
| **Nikolai Bernstein** | Degrees-of-freedom problem, variability, **essential vs. non-essential variables** | Motor control, constraints-led coaching |

Moyer's two structural points: **Zatsiorsky and Verkhoshansky were Bernstein's students**, so the same motor-control ideas run through Soviet biomechanics and special-strength methods; and **Michael Yessis** is the bridge through which much of this reached US practice (and Moyer).

**Why it works** — Knowing the source tells you the original purpose, population and limits of an idea, so you can tell a genuine advance from a re-labelled old one. Moyer's stronger claim — that modern research (thigh angular velocity, pawback, the two-mass model) **mostly rediscovers Soviet findings** — is his opinion. He supports it with side-by-side slides, not a systematic comparison, and the Soviet papers he relies on (largely *Soviet Sports Review* translations) are hard to check.

**When to apply** — A new sprint concept arrives with a new name. Building a reading list for a young staff member. Explaining to a sport coach why a special-strength exercise looks the way it does.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a hierarchy of authority. Several biographical details in the lecture are unverified or look wrong (for instance, the claim that Bondarchuk's athletes took every Olympic hammer medal for three Games; see the ingest digest). Soviet work was done in a closed system with limited peer review and state-sponsored doping; it is a source to trace, not a standard to defer to. The table is also Moyer's selection — Western lines (for example Weyand, Clark, Mann) are absent by design.

**Example** — A staff hears "thigh angular velocity" at a clinic. The lineage points them to Zatsiorsky-lab work on hip-flexor fatigue and thigh height, which predates it, and they read both before buying new equipment for it.

**Related** — [[framework--essential-vs-nonessential-variables-in-sprint-observation]] — the Bernstein → Verkhoshansky line applied to sprinting. [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] — Bompa's version of the Matveyev general/specific split; agreement.

#### thomas-2015-an-investigation-into-the-relationship-between-maximum-isometric-strength-and-vertical-jum.md
## Key findings

- Absolute IMTP impulses at 100–300 ms correlated with CMJ peak force (r=.63–.64, p≤.01), SJ peak force (r=.56–.58, p≤.01), CMJ peak power (r=.49–.51, p≤.05), and SJ peak power (r=.59–.60, p≤.01); correlations with jump height were near zero and nonsignificant. `[Table 3, p. 4]`
- Stronger and weaker groups differed in relative IMTP peak force (38.72±2.08 vs 30.40±4.01 N/kg, p=.01, d=2.60) and relative maximum RFD (172.59±37.64 vs 103.12±35.95 N/kg/s, p=.01, d=1.89). `[Table 7, p. 6]`
- They did not differ significantly in CMJ height (0.33±0.05 vs 0.36±0.05 m, p=.19) or SJ height (0.29±0.06 vs 0.33±0.05 m, p=.14). `[Table 7, p. 6]`
- Relative IMTP impulse measures were not significantly associated with vertical-jump performance measures in this sample. `[Table 3, p. 4]`

#### hanson-2007-acute-effects-of-heavy-and-light-load-squat-exercise-on-the-kinetic-measures-of-vertical-j.md
## Key findings

- Tables show very similar pre- and post-squat values across both loading conditions. [p. 4]
- The protocol did not produce a clear enhancement in the measured jump kinetics. [p. 5]
- The authors noted that recovery timing may have allowed potentiation to dissipate, especially after lighter loading. [p. 5]
- Movement specificity and the balance between fatigue and potentiation were plausible moderators. [p. 5]

#### jandacka-2008-a-regression-model-to-determine-load-for-maximum-power-output.md
## Key findings

- For the acceleration phase, estimated optimal bench-press loads were 56 ± 9% 1RM in men and 63 ± 8% 1RM in women. [p. 11]
- Corresponding countermovement-squat loads were 47 ± 9% of maximum dynamic strength in men and 54 ± 9% in women. [p. 11]
- Significant sex and exercise effects indicated that a single universal percentage could not represent every task or group. [p. 11]
- The authors recommended linking load to the measured force-velocity-power relationship rather than relying only on 1RM percentage. [p. 11]

#### hirayama-2014-acute-effects-of-an-ascending-intensity-squat-protocol-on-vertical-jump-performance.md
## Key findings

- Jump height increased about 4.3% after 60% 1-RM, 6.7% after 80% 1-RM, and 10.0% after the maximal isometric squat. [p. 3]
- The control condition showed no significant change across trials. [p. 3]
- The authors attributed the comparatively large response to recovery timing, athlete strength, final intensity, and cumulative exposure. [p. 4]

## Limitations and applicability

kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip.md
## Key findings

- Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. [p. 5]
- Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. [p. 5]
- Physical-education students showed the largest relative jump difference despite not being the highest-performing jump group, whereas most athlete groups had broadly similar values. [p. 6]
- The relative difference was moderately associated with countermovement-jump height across the full sample (r = 0.41) but was not associated with squat-jump height (r = 0.03); this association does not identify the mechanism producing the difference. [p. 6]

chapter: "3.4.5"
**What it is** — Coordination changes during a movement can take three forms (Averianov,
1963; Moikin, 1964): a change in the sequence of muscle groups participating, a change in
the number of muscle groups participating, and a change in the relative degree of
participation of different muscles. In complex multi-joint movements, the resulting force
does not equal the sum of the individual maximum tensions each contributing muscle group
is capable of. The authors' rowing example (Table 3.9, Egorov, 1966): the largest summed
force a rower develops occurs at the beginning of the stroke, even though the legs are
working at a disadvantageous knee and hip angle at that instant. However, the percentage
utilisation of absolute strength (the summed force actually produced relative to the
summed maximum each contributing muscle group could individually produce) is also largest
at that same instant. The authors' reading: disadvantageous conditions for one muscle
group's work can be compensated by more advantageous conditions for another's, through
effective coordination of contributory actions (here, the back muscles compensating for
#### principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains.md
chapter: "1"
**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)

**Why it works** — Inference: force output can rise before cross-sectional area change
translates into more strength through improved recruitment, firing rate, and coordination
of the muscle already present. Early strength gains outpacing measurable hypertrophy is a
replicated finding in resistance training research outside this text; whether hypertrophy
itself contributes meaningfully to early strength gains, versus being purely downstream, is
an active debate (Loenneke et al. 2019 vs. Taber et al. 2019, both Sports Med), which is
why this entry is capped at `supported` rather than `proven` for the broader "not muscle
#### framework--types-of-maximal-strength.md
chapter: "1"
**What it is** — The authors (citing Zatsiorsky) separate "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further

ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
